In his first public appearance after an election that soundly repudiated his policies, President Donald Trump turned to a topic both familiar and, given the context, surprising
By GARY FIELDS Associated Press and LISA MASCARO Associated Press

WASHINGTON -- In his first public appearance after an election that soundly repudiated his policies, President Donald Trump turned to a topic both familiar and, given the context, surprising: not his policies or politics, but his efforts to remake pieces of the city that is the backdrop to his presidency.

Despite Trump’s affinity for project management, though, with Democrats taking control of Congress, the work the administration is doing to change the physical face of the District of Columbia is sure to face far more roadblocks than it did for the first two years of his second term.

From the renaming of and renovation plans for the Kennedy Center to remaking a public golf course and erecting an arch 100 feet (30.48 meters) taller than the Statue of Liberty without its pedestal, the president has been deeply involved in how D.C. looks. Democrats have voiced opposition but, in terms of power, have been in the wilderness.

The potential collision point between an oppositional oversight from Democrats and the president's preoccupation with the projects was evident in his last message to the American public before the election — and in his first afterward, too.

Both focused to some degree on his projects. On Monday, it was the reflecting pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial ; on Wednesday, it was a tour of the under-construction White House ballroom, where he talked columns and steel beams and Corinthian designs.

Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee with jurisdiction over the Interior Department that is involved with operations at parks and federal lands, spent much of the past year probing and questioning Trump’s projects, laying the groundwork for this moment.

“We’ve pushed back against vanity projects that seek to transform treasured public spaces into gaudy tributes to Trump. We exposed corruption, uncovered the efforts to hijack America’s 250th birthday, demanded accountability, and offered a compelling alternative governing vision grounded in science, fairness, environmental responsibility, and the rule of law,” Huffman said in a letter to colleagues seeking their support to be chairman.

As chairman with a strong Democratic majority, “I will ensure that the Committee’s full investigative and oversight authority is leveraged to uncover wrongdoing, demand accountability, and protect the public interest," he said.

Trump has been rushing the various projects, a point Virginia Democratic Rep. Don Beyer made Thursday at a public hearing when he opposed construction of the memorial arch the president has planned in Memorial Circle directly across the Memorial Bridge from the Lincoln Memorial.
"The appropriations process beginning Jan. 3 will be controlled by Democrats. That will be one of the ways Congressman Beyer will step in,” said Beyer’s spokesman Aaron Fritschner.
A less appreciated impact will be the change in who names the general counsel of the House. The House Speaker has that role, presumably Rep. Hakeem Jeffries.

While Democrats have joined in lawsuits opposing the various projects, their filings don't carry the weight of Congress as the minority. “You’ll see the new majority pulling back the balance of power that (House Speaker) Mike Johnson was willing to cede,” Fritschner said.

Beyer has already been a critic, Fritschner said, and cited other members who have signed on in amicus briefs. More than 120 witnesses were on hand for the National Capital Planning Commission meeting, which ran for 9 ½ hours late into Thursday night.

The commission gave the 250-foot (76-meter) arch its final approval on an 8-4 vote, before a federal judge stepped in before midnight to block the Trump administration from breaking ground for 14 days.

title_en: Judge temporarily halts building work on Trump’s triumphal arch
title_zh: Judge temporarily halts building work on Trump’s triumphal arch

body_en: Judge temporarily halts building work on Trump’s triumphal arch | Washington DC
Federal judge issues 14-day restraining order on any construction work on Washington monument, hours after it was approved by planning commission

A federal judge has halted construction work on Donald Trump’s towering triumphal arch for 14 days, a major setback for one of the president’s most prominent projects in his vision to remake Washington.

The temporary restraining order was issued by US district judge Tanya Chutkan in the early hours of Friday. It followed a series of steps taken on Thursday by the government, including the final approval of the 250-foot-high (76-meter) arch by the National Capital Planning Commission in an 8-4 vote after a nine-hour hearing where dozens of witnesses opposed the construction.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face greater scrutiny after the Democrats gained control of Congress.
DoJ says Trump’s proposed 250ft arch would be completed after end of his term

The administration had said the work on the arch could begin as soon as the approval and the interior department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.

In issuing the delay, Chutkan granted the request of the latest plaintiffs in lawsuits challenging the arch. Chutkan also consolidated lawsuits from the District of Columbia and Virginia with a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian.
It’s unclear how much the project will cost, or how it will be paid for, although some estimates have reached as high as $100m.

The vote by the planning commission on Thursday came after nine and a half hours and scores of people opposing it. The vote by the commission broke along federal and local lines. Those in favor work for the administration or are connected to the president, who was pushing for the immediate construction. Opponents represented the city of Washington.

The remote, call-in hearing – which crashed repeatedly in the first few hours and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section – drew witnesses who gave impassioned comments opposing an arch that they said would destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington national cemetery, where hundreds of thousands of fallen service members and military veterans are buried.
The panel’s Trump-appointed chair launched the meeting with a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.
“President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it’s important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments,” said Mark Paoletta, the commission’s chair.

As Trump has often remarked, “the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London,” said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget.

Commissioner Paul Ingrassia, a lawyer for the General Services Administration, said the arch was “not about politics. It’s about remembrance. It’s about celebrating our history. It’s about commemorating veterans. And it’s really something that’s a noble tribute to our nation and something that we can all rally behind.”

But DC city council member Phil Mendelson, who also serves on the planning panel, said the project had not received required approval from Congress, nor had Congress appropriated any money for it. The plan submitted to the commission does not include a reference to military use cited by Trump and other administration officials, Mendelson said.
“We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plans,” he said.
Representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal.

“This arch would dishonor America,” Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch “a tribute to Donald Trump,” not veterans, as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself.

title_en: A judge blocks construction of Trump's arch moments after it won federal approval
title_zh: A judge blocks construction of Trump's arch moments after it won federal approval
summary: The Trump administration hoped to begin construction immediately after a federal panel approved its arch late Thursday. But just after midnight, the judge issued an order blocking work for 14 days.
summary_zh: The Trump administration hoped to begin construction immediately after a federal panel approved its arch late Thursday. But just after midnight, the judge issued an order blocking work for 14 days.
body_en: Demonstrators stand at Memorial Circle to protest President Trump's proposed arch on Thursday night as a federal panel heard hours of testimony from concerned citizens. It voted to approve the structure. Tom Brenner/Getty Images hide caption
A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's arch, stopping work the administration had hoped to begin immediately.

Just before midnight Friday, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order — finalized and made public minutes later - barring the government from any construction work for 14 days, granting a request filed days earlier by the governments of D.C. and Virginia .

She laid out her reasoning in a 33-page opinion , in which she scrutinized the administration's competing justifications for the arch — particularly its sudden emphasis on national security — and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The 250-foot arch would stand in Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery.
Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction

Trump administration officials have said work would take place 20 hours a day, year-round, for two to three years. In addition to questioning the arch's legality, D.C. and Virginia argue the construction would cause all sorts of financial and logistical disruptions.
"The threatened harms will materialize as soon as construction begins, in part because the traffic disruptions will occur immediately," Chutkan agreed.

Chutkan's ruling came less than two hours after a federal planning commission packed with presidential allies granted final approval to the arch in an 8-4 vote. The National Capital Planning Commission heard nearly eight hours of impassioned pleas from veterans, lawmakers, residents and concerned citizens opposed to the structure.
The Trump administration had previously told the court it could begin excavation work that same day, despite lacking authorization from Congress and an expanding legal challenge.

A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued the government earlier this year, arguing that an arch is unlawful without Congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. The Democratic governments of D.C. and Virginia jointly filed a similar lawsuit last weekend.
Chutkan consolidated the lawsuits and asked the government to notify the court within an hour of commission approval, setting the stage for an 11th-hour ruling.

Thursday started with a protest on Memorial Circle, where dozens of people spoke against the arch. The grass underfoot was already marked with white paint. Lawyers for the government told the court in a midday filing that the lines were painted on Saturday by its designated construction firm, seemingly without authorization from the National Park Service.
The commission meeting began at 1 p.m. It was held virtually because of the high volume of public testimony: 131 people were signed up to speak.

Just minutes into public testimony, the livestream crashed, lengthening the meeting by about an hour until it was restored. Over the course of nearly nine hours, commissioners heard from dozens of veterans and their relatives, Democratic lawmakers, historic preservation experts and concerned citizens from D.C. and beyond.
Trump aims to leave a physical legacy in D.C., bulldozing norms along the way

Among their many concerns , critics said the structure would obstruct an important view , insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to the notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They have questions about its legality and its cost, which the administration has not confirmed.
Many see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital — and described Democrats' midterm sweep as a referendum against it.

"Leaving aside all of the legitimate concerns and challenges about the required approvals, funding, land use, single-source bidding, and peer review, the American people spoke this past Tuesday at the ballot box," said former D.C. resident Emi Yamauchi. "They said enough vanity projects, enough corruption, enough Reflecting Pool travesties."
Only a handful of speakers offered support for the arch, including Republican Reps. Andrew Clyde of Georgia and Brian Mast of Florida, both of whom are veterans.

The Democrats’ stunning midterm victory should broaden Australia’s alliance with the US, observers say, even as a new power base emerges in Washington, affecting Aukus, datacentre development and relations with China.

Cabinet ministers, diplomats and Australia’s defence industrial sector closely watched the results this week, with control of the US Congress flipping to the Democrats and the outlook for Donald Trump’s final two years in office badly dinted.
Bruce Wolpe on what Trump will do after the ‘profound result’ of the US midterms - podcast

Public fury over rising living costs, particularly fuel prices, and the impact of datacentres, were also two factors in the midterms results that carry warnings for the Australian government, analysts said.
Bruce Wolpe, a senior fellow at the United States Studies Centre, said Trump’s ability to rile up voters had been undermined by cost of living.
Wolpe said the Albanese government was taking a hit because of the economic fallout from the Iran war.
“I think a lot of people are wondering what does this [Australian] government do?” he said. “Have they lost control of the economy?
“In January, before the Iran war, the outlook looked pretty good. But now, after going through a budget process and the war … people are just very uncertain as to where this is going to end up.
“It is not an immediately solvable problem, and people really dislike it.”
Westpac’s head of international economics, Elliot Clarke, said the landslide midterms results had “dramatically changed” the outlook for the Iran war, which could affect the economy in Australia.
“It has changed the ‘atmospherics’ around the Middle East conflict,” he said. “It’s positive news.”
There was a steep drop in the global oil price as the election results filtered out. The Brent crude benchmark, which had threatened to pass its April peak, has instead plunged by 20%.
More confidence in a potential resolution in the Middle East would also help curb inflation and help central banks hold back on rate hikes, according to Clarke.
“It definitely changes the calculus,” he said.
Coalition frontbencher Andrew Hastie said the results showed economic messaging was critical.

“People feel worse off after tariffs and after the war in Iran, and Donald Trump has said a few times now that he doesn’t really care,” he told 2GB. “Our job is always to deliver better outcomes for the Australian people.”

Arthur Sinodinos, a former ambassador to Washington, said the change on Capitol Hill was a chance for Australian officials to progress policy goals with both US parties, and to consider the relationship beyond the 2028 presidential election.

title_en: Trump focuses on White House decor for second straight day in post-midterm remarks
title_zh: Trump focuses on White House decor for second straight day in post-midterm remarks
summary: The president signed a proclamation that he said would prevent major changes to the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room by future presidents without congressional approval.
summary_zh: The president signed a proclamation that he said would prevent major changes to the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room by future presidents without congressional approval.
body_en: President Donald Trump is using his postelection public appearances to talk about the lasting physical changes he hopes to leave behind at the White House .
In the two days since Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections, Trump has spoken twice in public. Both times he focused on rooms and renovations at the White House.
On Thursday, Trump signed a proclamation that designates the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room as a national monument in an effort to block any significant changes to them by future presidents.

“We’re going to be declaring it a national monument, and we’re going to send it over to Congress to have it ratified,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “It won’t be able to be taken down, destroyed, touched or anything else.”

Trump, who later took questions from reporters about other topics, said any “major modifications” to the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room would have to be approved by Congress, adding that he hopes “the people in Congress will be smart enough not to let that happen.”

The White House has officially been a U.S. National Historic Landmark since 1960. Trump wrote in the proclamation that “the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance.”

The signing ceremony came a day after Trump spoke to reporters at the construction site for the new White House ballroom he’s building. Even though it was his first time addressing the media publicly after the Democrats swept several seats in deep red states to secure control of Congress, he focused his comments on the ballroom.

“I’m doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America and it’s got to be pristine — it’s got to be perfect,” Trump said, adding that he felt “it would be appropriate to have the media here.”

Unlike the ballroom project, which involved demolishing the historic East Wing and has attracted criticism from preservation groups , the Oval Office often undergoes cosmetic changes with each new administration.
When Trump returned to office last year, he completely redecorated the Oval Office , filling it with his signature favorite: lots and lots of gold.

The proclamation signed Thursday states that future presidents would still be able to “redecorate” the Oval Office and “select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications,” as long as they don’t “substantially impair the monument’s historic structure or architectural character.”
In discussing the proclamation, Trump also emphasized the “victories” he has achieved in the Oval Office, though he added, “I mean, there’s been some mistakes, too.” He didn’t elaborate.
Asked what he hopes Congress will focus on while Republicans still hold the majority for the next two months, Trump brought it back to himself.
“It’s been a tremendous two years. I don’t think there’s ever been a president that’s done more,” he said, speaking of his efforts at the border and on the stock market.
Trump’s final campaign message, on Monday, also centered in large part on his renovation efforts.

That speech was held at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool , which has been closed since July because of “botched” renovations made after Trump requested upgrades. He spent the majority of Monday’s remarks touting the pool’s reopening and his other renovation efforts around Washington.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

body_en: Trump signs proclamation to try to prevent changes to gold-covered Oval Office | Donald Trump
President seeks to make Oval Office a national monument to ensure designs are not ‘ripped down by stupid people’

Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces which he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.

In the days since his party suffered historic defeats in the midterm elections, the president has seemingly turned his attention to the many renovation projects he has begun across the nation’s capital. Sitting behind the Resolute Desk on Thursday, Trump declared the Oval Office a “national monument”.
“I’m going to be signing a document which will make them into a landmark for the ages,” he told reporters in the gold-covered Oval Office.

According to the president, the proclamation would ensure the West Wing rooms would not be “touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape”.
“I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come and take it down and try and do something with it,” he said.

“Every once in a while they’ll look and they’ll say, oh, maybe what we’ll do is we’ll put some glass up that’s a little bit better or something, and I say no, you’re not going to do anything. We’re going to leave this as it is,” he continued.
“If anyone ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you’ll call me wherever I may be, and I will come back here and I will make sure it never happens.”

Since returning to office, Trump has embarked on a series of White House “beautification” projects, most notably the demolition of the East Wing to make way for a $600m ballroom , as well the building of a permanent granite helipad on the South Lawn.

Speaking to reporters from the Oval Office, the president defended his wider renovation work at the White House, saying the building’s exterior had suffered from years of deterioration. He pointed to cracked windows, damaged stonework and broken decorative features, saying he had paid for repairs and hired skilled workers to restore them.
“When you looked at that wall one year ago, it was badly damaged from years of service,” he said, adding that exterior columns had also been in “horrible shape”.

On the desk next to where he signed the proclamation was a red baseball cap emblazoned with the word “Veto” – an explicit reminder of his threat to block the legislative priorities and bills passed by the new Democratic-controlled Congress next year.

Democrats made significant gains in several traditionally Republican states where Trump had previously won, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa, by campaigning on issues including affordability and tackling corruption, while also securing control of Congress.

Trump’s opulent redesign of the Oval Office has drawn criticism, including from former president Barack Obama, who recently joked that “he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”
Obama’s remark prompted a coordinated response from the White House, with treasury secretary Scott Bessent appearing to hit back by dining at a Cheesecake Factory.

In a final appeal ahead of the midterm elections, Trump held a press conference highlighting the delayed results of his $14m renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, while blaming Joe Biden for the algae that had accumulated in its waters.
“This was in the Biden era … Look, it’s not an easy thing. The algae is brutal. It forms easily. All you saw was dirt and filth and paper and everything else for years,” Trump said on Monday.
Two days later, as the scale of his party’s staggering losses came into focus, Trump led a media tour of the White House Ballroom construction site, where he marveled at the renovations to come.
body_zh: 特朗普签署公告，试图阻止金色椭圆形办公室发生变化|唐纳德·特朗普
总统寻求将椭圆形办公室打造成国家纪念碑，以确保设计不会“被愚蠢的人撕毁”
唐纳德·特朗普周四签署了一份公告，表示将阻止未来的政府改变他对椭圆形办公室和内阁会议室的设计，他宣称这些空间是应该保护的国家古迹。
自从他的政党在中期选举中遭受历史性失败以来，总统似乎将注意力转向了他在首都开始的许多改造项目。周四，特朗普坐在坚决办公桌后面，宣布椭圆形办公室为“国家纪念碑”。
“我将签署一份文件，使它们成为千古的里程碑，”他在金色椭圆形办公室对记者说。
总统表示，该公告将确保西翼的房间不会“被任何人触碰、破坏、被愚蠢的人撕毁，以建造形状略有不同的东西”。
“我只是认为非常重要的是不允许任何人过来把它拆下来并尝试用它做点什么，”他说。
“每隔一段时间，他们就会看一下，然后说，哦，也许我们要做的就是加一些玻璃，这样会好一点或者什么，我说不，你什么也不做。我们将保持原样，”他继续说道。
“如果有人决定来开始拆除墙壁，无论我在哪里，你都会给我打电话，我会回到这里，我将确保它永远不会发生。”
自重返办公室以来，特朗普开始实施一系列白宫“美化”项目，其中最著名的是拆除东翼，为耗资6亿美元的宴会厅腾出空间，以及在南草坪修建永久性花岗岩直升机停机坪。
总统在椭圆形办公室向记者发表讲话，为他在白宫进行的更广泛的翻修工作进行了辩护，称该建筑的外观多年来一直在恶化。他指着破裂的窗户、损坏的石雕和破损的装饰，说他已经支付了维修费用，并聘请了熟练工人来修复它们。
“当你一年前看那堵墙时，你会发现它因多年的使用而受到严重损坏，”他说，并补充说外部柱子也“形状可怕”。
在他签署公告的地方旁边的桌子上有一顶红色棒球帽，上面印有“否决”一词——明确提醒人们，他威胁要阻止明年民主党控制的新国会通过的立法优先事项和法案。
民主党在特朗普之前获胜的几个传统共和党州取得了重大进展，包括德克萨斯州、堪萨斯州、南卡罗来纳州和爱荷华州，他们在负担能力和解决腐败等问题上进行了竞选活动，同时也确保了对国会的控制。
特朗普对椭圆形办公室的华丽重新设计引起了批评，其中包括前总统巴拉克·奥巴马(Barack Obama)，他最近开玩笑说“他让白宫看起来像萨达姆·侯赛因(Saddam Hussein)开了一家芝士蛋糕工厂。到处都是黄金。”
奥巴马的言论引发了白宫的协调反应，财政部长斯科特·贝森特似乎通过在芝士蛋糕工厂用餐来进行回击。
在中期选举前的最后呼吁中，特朗普举行了一场新闻发布会，强调了他耗资 1400 万美元翻修林肯纪念堂倒影池的延迟结果，同时将水域中藻类堆积的原因归咎于乔·拜登。
“那是在拜登时代……看，这不是一件容易的事。藻类很残酷。它很容易形成。多年来你看到的都是泥土、污物、纸张和其他一切，”特朗普周一表示。
两天后，随着共和党惊人损失的规模成为人们关注的焦点，特朗普带领媒体参观了白宫宴会厅建筑工地，他对那里即将进行的翻修工程感到惊叹。

Here are the House races left on the map Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined. Here's where things stand in the races that are waiting to be called by the AP.
Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined and several races are still outstanding.

A few in California are being contested by two candidates in the same party. So it's clear which party will hold the seat, even if it's not clear who will win. Others are too close to call or there aren't enough ballots counted to know which candidate will prevail. In many places in the country, it takes a while to count votes . That's normal and expected.

In the Senate, there are two races outstanding, Alaska and Mississippi. Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting and no candidate in the four-person race has achieved a 50% majority in the count, it may proceed to another round of counting later this month. Mississippi uses a more traditional electoral system but a large number of provisional ballots — called affidavit ballots in the state — are taking time to count. Less than 2,000 votes separate the top two candidates in that race.

加利福尼亚州的一些州正在由同一政党的两名候选人竞争。因此，即使尚不清楚谁会获胜，但哪个政党将占据席位还是很清楚的。其他候选人的胜负势均力敌，或者没有统计到足够的选票，无法确定哪位候选人会获胜。在该国许多地方，计票需要一段时间。这是正常的，也是意料之中的。

在参议院，有两个竞选悬而未决：阿拉斯加和密西西比。由于阿拉斯加采用排名选择投票，四人竞选中没有候选人在计票中获得 50% 多数，因此本月晚些时候可能会进行另一轮计票。密西西比州使用更传统的选举制度，但大量临时选票（该州称为宣誓选票）需要时间来计票。这场竞选中排名前两名的候选人之间的票数相差不到 2,000 张。

title_en: Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine
title_zh: 梅拉尼娅·特朗普吹捧她在俄罗斯和乌克兰之间斡旋达成的罕见协议
summary: The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.
summary_zh: 俄罗斯占领的奥列什基市暂停六天之际，政府正加紧努力达成结束乌克兰战争的协议
body_en: Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 05: First lady Melania Trump gives hand written letters to Russian special envoy and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund Kirill Dmitrievon (L) and Ukrainian human rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets (C) to deliver to their presidents during an event on a temporary Russia-Ukraine ceasefire at the White House on November 5, 2026 in Washington, DC. Samuel Corum/Getty Images hide caption
First lady Melania Trump hosted a rare meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to recognize a temporary ceasefire in southeastern Ukraine .
The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.
"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the divisions of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace."

Trump has accomplished something that has so far eluded her husband - helping broker a temporary ceasefire and bringing together representatives of the two sides in acknowledgement of the human costs of the war.
The White House sees it as a diplomatic breakthrough, but some European analysts worry the efforts can backfire.
The temporary reprieve, which expired on Sunday, enabled humanitarian aid to reach the city while allowing hundreds of residents to be evacuated.
Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special envoy, thanked the first lady. He said Putin personally gave the instructions to ensure the successful implementation of the ceasefire.

"On behalf of President Putin, on behalf of the people of the Russian Federation, we would like to thank first lady Melania Trump for her distinguished humanitarian role in resolving a key situation and resolving this humanitarian issue," he said.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets presented Melania Trump with an award for her humanitarian work. The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, is Ukraine's highest award for women.
"I have only one request from all Ukrainian nation," Lubinets said, "please continue doing your wonderful work and support people."
The event comes just days before the U.S. leads a new round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week.
President Trump also met with Dmitriev at the White House.
Trump told reporters that the sides were close to reaching a deal.

"It's going to be an agreement. It's going to be a big agreement, ‌and ⁠it's going to involve more than Ukraine," he said. "I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's ⁠going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."

Heather Conley, who worked on European issues in President George W. Bush's State Department, supports all efforts to help suffering Ukrainians, but she also said the U.S. must be careful not to normalize Russia's bad behavior.

"In this White House ceremony, we were honoring the Russians that were the cause of both the occupation of Oleshky, the starvation of Oleshky, and now we're honoring them for allowing aid to come into Oleshky," said Conley, who is now a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. "The more we create this equivalency where the Russians and the Ukrainians are equal in this crisis, it is putting this thing upside down."
body_zh: 梅拉尼娅·特朗普吹捧她在俄罗斯和乌克兰之间斡旋达成的罕见协议。在俄罗斯占领的奥列什基市暂停六天之际，美国政府正在加紧努力，以达成结束乌克兰战争的协议。
华盛顿特区 - 11 月 5 日：第一夫人梅拉尼娅·特朗普于 2026 年 11 月 5 日在华盛顿特区白宫举行的俄罗斯-乌克兰临时停火活动期间，向俄罗斯特使兼俄罗斯直接投资基金负责人基里尔·德米特里冯（左）和乌克兰人权监察员德米特罗·鲁宾涅茨（中）递交了手写信，以便转交给两国总统。塞缪尔·科鲁姆/盖蒂图片社隐藏标题栏
第一夫人梅拉尼娅·特朗普在白宫主持了一次罕见的俄罗斯和乌克兰官员会面，承认乌克兰东南部的临时停火。
俄罗斯占领的奥列什基市暂停六天之际，美国政府正在加紧努力，以达成结束乌克兰战争的协议。
“我们选择了人性而不是战争，”第一夫人说。 “不可否认，无辜人民的生命必须超越战争的分歧。我希望奥列什基能够激发更大的和平。”
特朗普完成了她丈夫迄今为止未能完成的事情——帮助促成临时停火，并让双方代表聚集在一起，承认战争造成的人员伤亡。
白宫认为这是一次外交突破，但一些欧洲分析人士担心这些努力可能会适得其反。
周日到期的临时禁令使人道主义援助能够到达该市，同时使数百名居民得以疏散。
俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京的特使基里尔·德米特里耶夫向第一夫人表示感谢。他说，普京亲自作出指示，确保停火协议顺利实施。
他说：“我们谨代表普京总统，代表俄罗斯联邦人民，感谢第一夫人梅拉尼娅·特朗普在解决关键局势和这一人道主义问题方面所发挥的杰出人道主义作用。”
乌克兰人权监察员德米特罗·鲁比内茨向梅拉尼娅·特朗普颁发了人道主义工作奖。一级奥尔哈公主勋章是乌克兰授予女性的最高奖项。
鲁比涅茨说：“我只有一​​个来自乌克兰全国人民的请求，请继续做好你们出色的工作并支持人民。”
此次活动发生在美国下周在阿布扎比举行新一轮俄罗斯和乌克兰和平谈判的几天前。
特朗普总统还在白宫会见了德米特里耶夫。
特朗普告诉记者，双方即将达成协议。
“这将是一项协议。这将是一项重大协议，而且涉及的不仅仅是乌克兰，”他说。 “我什至可以说，这可能涉及整个欧洲。这将是一项重大而美好的协议，每个人都会感到兴奋。”
曾在乔治·W·布什总统的国务院负责欧洲问题的希瑟·康利支持一切帮助受苦受难的乌克兰人的努力，但她也表示，美国必须小心，不要让俄罗斯的不良行为正常化。
“在这次白宫仪式上，我们向那些造成奥列什基被占领和饥饿的俄罗斯人致敬，现在我们向他们致敬，因为他们允许援助进入奥列什基，”现任美国企业研究所高级研究员的康利说。 “我们越是创造出俄罗斯人和乌克兰人在这场危机中平等的对等关系，就会把事情颠倒过来。”

title_en: How Democrats plan to investigate the Trump administration after their midterm wins
title_zh: 民主党计划在中期选举获胜后如何调查特朗普政府
summary: With their new majorities, Democrats will have at their disposal the full investigatory powers of the Congress, which include the ability to subpoena records and compel individuals to testify.
summary_zh: 凭借新的多数席位，民主党将拥有国会的全部调查权，其中包括传票的能力
body_en: How Democrats plan to investigate the Trump administration after their midterm wins With their new majorities, Democrats will have at their disposal the full investigatory powers of the Congress, which include the ability to subpoena records and compel individuals to testify.
With their new majorities, Democrats will have at their disposal the full investigatory powers of the Congress, which include the ability to subpoena records and compel individuals to testify.

Democrats will be able to pass bills on their own when the new Congress is sworn in in January, but they can't make President Trump sign those bills into law. One thing that they can do on their own - investigate, investigate, investigate. NPR's Eric McDaniel is here in the studio now to share more about that part of the Democratic governing agenda. Hi, Eric.

CHANG: Howdy, howdy. OK. So it has been a few years since we've had different parties in control of the White House and Congress, and that always does result in investigation. So can we just take a moment to remind everyone what this part of congressional work is all about?

MCDANIEL: This is so important. I don't think we can be too basic here. Look, Congress has a few key functions. They pass laws. They direct tax dollars, the power of the purse, and they conduct oversight of the executive branch...

MCDANIEL: ...Investigations. That's the third bucket. They have the authority to force documents to be turned over, to make people come and testify under oath, to hold people accountable in the courts if they refuse. And these have been used to great effect through U.S. history, right? The Watergate-era investigations exposed big cover-up schemes by the Nixon administration. The Reagan administration selling weapons to Iran to fund Nicaraguan rebels, the 9/11 Commission, the CIA black site torture report in the 2010s. And with government corruption at the top of the list of voter concerns, it makes sense that this would be a tool Democrats are prioritizing.
CHANG: OK. And do we know what they will focus on come January?

MCDANIEL: There are some things people are probably already thinking about as they listen. The president and his family have gotten much richer during the second term. The Justice Department's handling of the documents tied to late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein also going to be a focus. But there are things you might not be thinking about that I'd argue may be even more important for the health of democracy.

MCDANIEL: Right. I mentioned at the top Congress has power of the purse, right? The president and his Office of Management and Budget director, though, Russ Vought, have twice ignored how Congress directed that spending. They either didn't spend it on things that Congress said they should or did other things with it. And that's a very big deal. The power of the purse to decide how money is spent is the constitutional power that underpins all other congressional powers. So if the presidency manages to subsume that, what is Congress really there for?
Second, I'd say the Iran war and just the use of the military generally. Remember, the Pentagon...

MCDANIEL: ...Has been striking what they describe as drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific. The president and his secretary of defense have never made the case to the American public about the war in Iran. And Congress is supposed to authorize all military conflicts. That's never happened with either of these campaigns. So expect to see deep looks at both of those things.

CHANG: OK. I hear you on all of these potential investigations, but the thing is, Eric, the cost of living was the huge concern in this election - right? - which is much more concrete than, say, something like public corruption.
CHANG: So do you think there is any risk that these investigations could come off as retribution, and only that, against the Trump administration rather than actual oversight and accountability?

MCDANIEL: Totally. I think that's a huge risk. But there are a lot of ways that investigations can look that just aren't necessarily apparent efforts to undermine the presidency. In the post-Watergate era, Jimmy Carter would say this thing, that the public deserved a government as good as its people. And I think the most successful congressional investigations had been able to work toward that goal of transparency.

One example that looms large in my mind, for example, there are allegations that the U.S. military bombed a school in Iran in the early days of the offensive against that country. More than a hundred kids are said to have died. That isn't a topic with a clear partisan lean. It's about establishing a factual record about what happened and what might need to change about how we conduct strikes going forward.

CHANG: I mean, investigations can feel retaliatory. Arguably, that's how so many people characterize the two impeachments of Trump during his first term in office. So could they go down that road again, you think?

MCDANIEL: I just don't see it happening. As best I can tell, there's no momentum, right? And I think the lesson that this has failed as a political strategy is one Democrats have taken on board. But Trump is less popular now than ever before. He's on his way out of office. There's no threat of another term losing. That means the political upside, that they could prohibit him from serving in office again, is gone. And they have such a huge agenda - right? - healthcare, housing, tariffs, education, climate. It's a big world out there, and, you know, they might need to do some table setting for 2028.

title_en: White House event reveals Ukraine and Russia share one goal: flattering Melania
title_zh: 白宫活动显示乌克兰和俄罗斯有一个共同目标：奉承梅拉尼娅
summary: As war rages on in Kyiv and other cities, the first lady celebrates her single-city ceasefire with Russian and Ukrainian envoys Beaming from a podium in the White House’s Grand Foyer, Melania Trump welcomed senior Russian and Ukrainian officials on Thursday to
summary_zh: 随着基辅和其他城市的战争愈演愈烈，第一夫人在讲台上与俄罗斯和乌克兰特使庆祝单城停火
body_en: As war rages on in Kyiv and other cities, the first lady celebrates her single-city ceasefire with Russian and Ukrainian envoys

B eaming from a podium in the White House’s Grand Foyer, Melania Trump welcomed senior Russian and Ukrainian officials on Thursday to celebrate a ceasefire in an embattled Ukrainian town for which she has become the unlikeliest broker.

The evacuation from Oleshky, a frontline Ukrainian town now occupied by Russia where 800 people lived through a protracted humanitarian crisis, may seem like a sideshow at this point in the war. Russian missiles and drones continue to rain down on Kyiv and other major cities, and a single Russian strike described as a “double-tap” bombing killed 40 people in Zaporizhzhia on Wednesday.

So it could have been easy to brush the White House meeting off as a chance for Ukraine and Russia to flatter the first lady. And flatter her they did, praising her for her diplomatic acumen, delivering her state awards and even gifting her trinkets of thanks from the residents of Oleshky whom she saved. In case the subtext was not yet clear, a children’s drawing gifted by the Russian side was inscribed: “I love Melania.”

But there was real diplomatic juice in the room as Trump, a former model who has occupied a relatively quiet role in her husband’s second term as president, now played host to one of the highest-level gatherings of Russian and Ukrainian officials in recent months.

Kirill Dmitriev, the sanctioned head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund who regularly negotiates for Moscow, was seated next to Davyd Arakhamia, the head of Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party and a chief negotiator for Ukraine. Next to them were Ukraine’s Dmytro Lubinets and Russia’s Yana Lantratova, the respective human rights ombudspeople who have become an unlikely and respectful double act throughout the evacuation process.

The meeting came after a particularly bitter public feud between Zelenskyy and Trump, as the US cut intelligence sharing and satellite internet in recent weeks in an apparent effort to pressure Kyiv into capitulating. And the Trump administration’s plans with Russia are in peril after the midterms, with triumphant Democrats promising to investigate senior aides to Trump who had pitched Russia on business deals to end the war in Ukraine.

But everyone at the White House on Thursday was focused on feting Melania, whose role in brokering the ceasefire was extensively praised at every opportunity – even if her descriptions of reviewing de-mining plans and assessing evacuation routes strained belief.

As well as the drawing, Dmitriev extended her a personal expression of gratitude from Vladimir Putin, while on the Ukrainian side, Lubinets presented her with the order of Princess Olga, first class – one of the country’s highest honours. He also issued a general request: “Please continue to do your wonderful work and support people.”
Stepping into the role of diplomat and humanitarian, the first lady called for “humanity over war” and said that she hoped the limited ceasefire in the frontline town would “inspire greater peace”.

“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” she said. “Let us see Oleshky as a spark in a world of darkness, capable of illuminating the best in humanity. Build a powerful flame of peace, visible to the world. Ignite hope, foster cooperation and brighten a path toward lasting peace.”
Later, she handed personal letters to Dmitriev and Arakhamia to bring back to Putin and Zelenskyy.

Donald Trump didn’t attend, and didn’t have any public events on his schedule on Tuesday. Later in the day, he said he met with Dimitriev but not with Ukrainian officials, and refused to say what they discussed. The president’s absence from the White House event was conspicuous, both because of the high-profile guests, and because of his own well-known interest in being seen as a peacemaker. While he has publicly demanded the Nobel peace prize, on Thursday it was Melania who was being crowned the humanitarian-in-chief.

It was an unusual role for her. She has not taken part in high-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia before, and is said behind the scenes to have been critical of her husband’s heavy-handed approach to dealing with Ukraine.
But she has increasingly engaged in humanitarian efforts related to the conflict, first by working on a program that reunified more than 30 children displaced from their families during the conflict.

In Oleshky, she also claimed to have been involved in “every stage” of the planning. To do so, she said, she had “reviewed de-mining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles and medical resources”.
Now the White House has cast her as a dark horse diplomat.

“This unprecedented gathering marks the first time in US history that an American first lady has personally brought representatives of two nations actively at war together at the White House to pursue diplomatic and humanitarian objectives,” said Marc Beckman, an aide who is self-described as her exclusive senior adviser.
What’s clear is that at this moment both sides have recognised the need to keep Melania – and the testy Trump administration – onside.
body_zh: 随着基辅和其他城市的战争愈演愈烈，第一夫人与俄罗斯和乌克兰特使庆祝单城停火
周四，梅拉尼娅·特朗普在白宫大厅的讲台上满面笑容地欢迎俄罗斯和乌克兰高级官员，庆祝陷入困境的乌克兰小镇实现停火，而她已成为最不可能的掮客。
奥列什基是乌克兰前线城镇，现已被俄罗斯占领，那里有 800 人正在经历一场旷日持久的人道主义危机，从奥列什基的撤离在战争的这个阶段似乎只是一场余兴节目。俄罗斯导弹和无人机继续袭击基辅和其他主要城市，周三，俄罗斯一次被称为“双击”轰炸的袭击在扎波罗热造成 40 人死亡。
因此，很容易将白宫会议视为乌克兰和俄罗斯奉承第一夫人的机会。他们还奉承她，赞扬她的外交头脑，授予她国家奖项，甚至还赠送了她拯救的奥列什基居民的感谢礼物。如果潜台词还不清楚的话，俄罗斯方面赠送的一幅儿童画上写着：“我爱梅拉尼娅。”
但房间里确实充满了外交活力，因为特朗普曾是一名模特，在丈夫的第二个总统任期内扮演着相对安静的角色，现在主持了近几个月来俄罗斯和乌克兰官员最高级别的聚会之一。
经常为莫斯科进行谈判的俄罗斯直接投资基金负责人基里尔·德米特里耶夫坐在弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基的人民公仆党主席、乌克兰首席谈判代表达维德·阿拉卡米亚旁边。他们旁边是乌克兰的德米特罗·鲁宾涅茨（Dmytro Lubinets）和俄罗斯的亚娜·兰特拉托娃（Yana Lantratova），他们分别是人权监察员，在整个撤离过程中，他们成为了令人难以置信且令人尊敬的双重角色。
这次会议是在泽伦斯基和特朗普之间发生特别激烈的公开争执之后举行的，美国最近几周削减了情报共享和卫星互联网，显然是为了迫使基辅投降。特朗普政府与俄罗斯的计划在中期选举后面临危险，胜利的民主党人承诺调查特朗普的高级助手，这些助手曾向俄罗斯推销结束乌克兰战争的商业协议。
但周四，白宫的每个人都把注意力集中在庆祝梅拉尼娅身上，她在斡旋停火方面的作用一有机会就受到广泛赞扬——尽管她对审查排雷计划和评估疏散路线的描述令人难以置信。
除了绘画之外，德米特里耶夫还向她表达了弗拉基米尔·普京个人的谢意，而在乌克兰方面，卢宾涅茨则向她颁发了奥尔加公主一等勋章——这是该国的最高荣誉之一。他还发出了一个总体要求：“请继续做好你的出色工作并支持人们。”
第一夫人扮演外交官和人道主义者的角色，呼吁“以人道战胜战争”，并表示她希望前线城镇的有限停火能够“激发更大的和平”。
“我们可以共同创造比暂时停火更持久的东西，”她说。 “让我们将奥列什基视为黑暗世界中的一颗火花，能够照亮人类最好的一面。建立世界可见的强大和平之火。点燃希望，促进合作，照亮一条通往持久和平的道路。”
随后，她将私人信件交给德米特里耶夫和阿拉卡米亚，让他们带回给普京和泽连斯基。
唐纳德·特朗普没有出席，周二的日程上也没有任何公共活动。当天晚些时候，他说他会见了迪米特里耶夫，但没有会见乌克兰官员，并拒绝透露他们讨论的内容。总统缺席白宫活动很引人注目，这既是因为出席了备受瞩目的嘉宾，也是因为众所周知，他本人很想被视为和平缔造者。虽然他公开要求获得诺贝尔和平奖，但周四，梅拉尼娅被加冕为人道主义领袖。
这对她来说是一个不寻常的角色。她此前从未参加过乌克兰与俄罗斯之间的高层谈判，据说在幕后一直批评她丈夫对待乌克兰的高压手段。
但她越来越多地参与与冲突相关的人道主义工作，首先是参与一项项目，帮助 30 多名在冲突期间与家人流离失所的儿童团聚。
在奥列什基中，她还声称自己参与了规划的“每个阶段”。她说，为此，她“审查了排雷计划、航拍图像，评估了道路，并讨论了疏散路线、医院通道、车辆和医疗资源”。
现在白宫将她视为黑马外交官。
“这次史无前例的聚会标志着美国历史上第一次由美国第一夫人亲自将两个活跃交战国家的代表聚集在白宫，以追求外交和人道主义目标，”自称是她的独家高级顾问的助手马克·贝克曼(Marc Beckman)说。
显而易见的是，目前双方都认识到有必要让梅拉尼娅和脾气暴躁的特朗普政府站在一边。

title_en: Deep-red Kansas votes for change as patience wears thin with Trump: ‘The economy is really taking a beating’
title_zh: 随着对特朗普的耐心逐渐减弱，深红色的堪萨斯州投票支持变革：“经济确实受到了打击”
summary: Bills have soared in rural state buffeted by tariffs and war in Iran – and Democrat Adam Hamilton’s stunning upset shows how deep economic frustrations run Linda Olson always does her homework before voting – a trait she inherited from a family invested, and i
summary_zh: 受到关税和伊朗战争打击的农村州的账单飙升——民主党人亚当·汉密尔顿的令人震惊的不满表明了经济挫败感有多么严重
body_en: Bills have soared in rural state buffeted by tariffs and war in Iran – and Democrat Adam Hamilton’s stunning upset shows how deep economic frustrations run

L inda Olson always does her homework before voting – a trait she inherited from a family invested, and interested, in politics. Her father was a photographer who took portraits of political leaders in Washington, while her grandparents were farmers who cared deeply about their industry.

In 2024, Olson’s research led her to Donald Trump . She trusted that the then-former president would improve their economic realities in Junction City, Kansas – where she was born and raised – if he returned to the White House.

But two years later, life is just more expensive. Last winter, Olson was forced to spend $700 on medication while in between insurance plans, and skipped out on doses to stretch it out longer. Her grocery bills are unrecognizably high. And fuel prices are about a dollar per gallon more expensive than last year.
“I thought at the time that he was the better choice of what we had,” Olson said of Trump in 2024. Instead, he had been acting to “make himself richer instead of really helping the people”.

With frustrations like these looming large across the state, Kansans this week elected a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the US Senate for the first time in nearly a century. It was a stunning upset in what was, until recently, thought to be a reliably red stronghold.
“I’ve seen what Roger Marshall did over the eight years or so that he’s been doing this,” said Olson, of the defeated Republican senator. “And I thought, it’s time we get fresh blood up there.”

Hamilton won, in part, by flipping six counties that backed Trump in 2024 and Marshall in 2020 – a sign that, even in more remote, and traditionally conservative, areas, patience with Trump and the Republican party is wearing thin.

“Not everybody that voted for Trump is part of this cult of personality that Trump has tried to make the Republican party into,” said Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, located in one of those six flipped counties.
“There are certainly people in Kansas that are like that: they’re pretty conservative, but they’re not beholden to Trump. And so I think one of the things this election did is peel off those people.”

M ost of Kansas is made up of farmland, encompassing nearly 45m acres and employing nearly one in five Kansans. Pastures, dotted with grazing cows and their calves, hug the state’s highways. Junction City is surrounded by its famed toffee-colored prairies, so expansive that untouched grassland stretches out to the horizon on both sides of the interstate.

Kansans who ranch and farm here, in the most rural corners of the state, remain deeply Republican, according to Smith. But neighboring communities such as Junction City and Emporia, where he teaches, depend heavily on the agricultural economy and have felt the impact of the strains on farmers.
“The people that live here aren’t actually farmers,” he said. “And they’re more likely to swing over to the other party because the economy is really taking a beating.”
David Aguirre, a 25-year-old who was born and raised in Junction City, and works at a Mexican restaurant, El Patron Dos, said that when the rest of the county is suffering, so does his work.
“It has, like, a domino effect for families,” he said. “If they’re not doing their best, they’re not gonna come out to eat, and then that affects staff, and cooks, and so on.”

While grocery shopping on Wednesday afternoon, Janet Grimm, who considers herself an independent, lamented her rising bills. Everything she picked out from the aisles was tagged with a red and yellow “sale” sticker, a conscious choice she needs to make now.
Kansas Democrat’s pitch to voters amid historic Senate bid: ‘I’m gonna just fight like hell’

Checking out with just a handful of items – eggs, chicken, some deli meat, two cucumbers and powdered sugar for the banana bread she was planning on making later that day – her total rang up to over $60.
Grimm voted for Hamilton, and felt hopefully that he would be able to improve the economy for people like her. “I really have faith that they’re going to do good,” she said.
body_zh: 受到关税和伊朗战争打击的农村州的账单飙升——民主党人亚当·汉密尔顿的令人震惊的不满表明了经济挫败感有多么严重
琳达·奥尔森（Linda Olson）总是在投票前做功课——这是她从一个对政治投资和感兴趣的家庭继承的特质。她的父亲是一位摄影师，为华盛顿的政治领导人拍摄肖像，而她的祖父母是农民，非常关心他们的行业。
2024 年，奥尔森的研究让她找到了唐纳德·特朗普。她相信，如果这位时任前总统回到白宫，他将改善她出生和长大的堪萨斯州章克申城的经济现实。
但两年后，生活变得更加昂贵。去年冬天，奥尔森在保险计划期间被迫花费 700 美元购买药物，并且为了延长服药时间而跳过了服药。她的杂货账单高得难以想象。燃油价格比去年每加仑贵一美元左右。
奥尔森在谈到 2024 年的特朗普时说：“我当时认为他是我们所拥有的更好的选择。”相反，他一直在“让自己变得更富有，而不是真正帮助人民”。
由于类似的挫败感在全州范围内日益凸显，堪萨斯州本周选举民主党人亚当·汉密尔顿进入美国参议院，这是近一个世纪以来的首次。对于直到最近还被认为是可靠的红色据点的地方来说，这是一个令人震惊的意外。
“我看到了罗杰·马歇尔在过去八年左右的时间里所做的事情，他一直在这样做，”奥尔森在谈到这位落败的共和党参议员时说道。 “我想，是时候我们为那里注入新鲜血液了。”
汉密尔顿获胜的部分原因是在 2024 年推翻了支持特朗普的六个县，在 2020 年推翻了支持马歇尔的六个县——这表明，即使在更偏远、传统上保守的地区，人们对特朗普和共和党的耐心也在逐渐减弱。
位于这六个翻转县之一的恩波里亚州立大学政治学教授迈克尔·史密斯说：“并不是所有投票给特朗普的人都是特朗普试图让共和党陷入这种个人崇拜的一部分。”
“堪萨斯州肯定有人是这样的：他们相当保守，但他们并不受制于特朗普。所以我认为这次选举所做的事情之一就是剥离了这些人。”
堪萨斯州大部分地区都是农田，占地近 4500 万英亩，雇用了近五分之一的堪萨斯人。牧场紧邻该州的高速公路，牧场上点缀着正在吃草的奶牛和它们的小牛。章克申城周围环绕着著名的太妃糖色大草原，其广阔无垠的草原一直延伸到州际公路两侧的地平线。
史密斯表示，在该州最农村的角落里放牧和务农的堪萨斯人仍然是坚定的共和党人。但他任教的章克申城和恩波里亚等邻近社区严重依赖农业经济，并感受到了农民承受压力的影响。
“住在这里的人实际上并不是农民，”他说。 “而且他们更有可能转向另一方，因为经济确实受到了打击。”
25 岁的戴维·阿吉雷 (David Aguirre) 在章克申城出生和长大，在一家墨西哥餐厅 El Patron Dos 工作，他说，当全县其他人都在受苦时，他的工作也是如此。
“这对家庭来说就像多米诺骨牌效应，”他说。 “如果他们没有尽力而为，他们就不会出来吃饭，这就会影响员工、厨师等。”
周三下午，在杂货店购物时，自认为是独立人士的珍妮特·格林 (Janet Grimm) 对自己不断上涨的账单感到遗憾。她从过道上挑选的所有东西都贴有红色和黄色的“促销”标签，这是她现在需要做出的有意识的选择。
堪萨斯州民主党在历史性的参议院竞选中向选民宣传：“我要拼命战斗”
只检查了几样东西——鸡蛋、鸡肉、一些熟食肉、两根黄瓜和她计划当天晚些时候制作香蕉面包的糖粉——她的总价就超过了 60 美元。
格林投票给了汉密尔顿，并希望他能够为像她这样的人改善经济。 “我真的相信他们会做好事，”她说。

title_en: Trump tries to get 2024 conviction in hush-money corruption case thrown out
title_zh: 特朗普试图推翻2024年封口费腐败案的定罪
summary: President’s lawyers ask appeals court to toss criminal trial verdict over $130,000 sent to Stormy Daniels Donald Trump’s legal team on Thursday continued efforts to get his 2024 conviction in the hush-money election corruption case thrown out. Attorneys for th
summary_zh: 总统律师要求上诉法院驳回周四发送给斯托米·丹尼尔斯唐纳德·特朗普法律团队的 13 万美元刑事审判判决
body_en: President’s lawyers ask appeals court to toss criminal trial verdict over $130,000 sent to Stormy Daniels
Donald Trump’s legal team on Thursday continued efforts to get his 2024 conviction in the hush-money election corruption case thrown out.

Attorneys for the US president are trying to persuade a New York appeals court to toss the criminal trial verdict from May 2024, when Trump was found guilty on all charges of falsifying business records in the hush-money corruption scheme to influence his eventual victory in the 2016 presidential election .

The felony conviction came after the jury agreed he altered records in order to obscure a $130,000 payment to buy the silence of adult film performer and producer Stormy Daniels . Trump mentioned the case again on social media as recently as September.

He was already the president-elect for his second term in office in early January 2025 when the judge in the case gave Trump an unconditional discharge, meaning he would remain a convicted felon but was given no jail time, fine or other penalty.
The president has always denied any wrongdoing and has turned to state and federal courts in hopes of unwinding the verdict. He was not expected to attend Thursday’s court session.

The trial involved the fee that Daniels received from Trump’s then fixer and lawyer, Michael Cohen , weeks before the 2016 election. The money bought, for a time, her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with Trump a decade earlier when he was already married to Melania Trump and she had given birth to his youngest son, Barron. Trump maintains that nothing sexual happened with Daniels.
However, then Trump’s company reimbursed Cohen in 2017, logging those payments as legal expenses.

Saying the transactions all were meant to keep unflattering information about Trump away from the electorate, prosecutors argue that he “orchestrated a conspiracy” that violated federal campaign finance laws, among others.

Trump’s lawyers argue there is only “weak” evidence that he even knew about Cohen’s dealings at the time. His trial attorneys also said that payments to Cohen were legal expenses and were merely to avoid embarrassing Trump’s family.

On Thursday, a panel of five appellate judges peppered prosecutors and Trump’s lawyer with questions, particularly about the defense’s argument that prosecutors’ legal theory was built on a shaky combination of alleged state and federal offenses.
The Manhattan district attorney’s office says the hush money was meant to keep unflattering information about Trump away from the 2016 electorate and broke the Federal Election Campaign Act (Feca).
Trump lawyer Robert Giuffra Jr told the judges that state prosecutors have no place tying a case to a federal election law. “We think it’s the most obvious ground for reversal,” he said.

Prosecutors argued otherwise, saying that they weren’t prosecuting an alleged federal campaign finance offense, but rather presenting it as a fact that drove what they claim was a conspiracy that led to phony records.
“So are you relying upon Feca in order to prove your falsifying business records (charge)?” asked Troy Webber, the judge.

“Only partially,” replied Steven Wu, the Manhattan assistant district attorney, adding that it was “important only to show that the purpose for the falsifying business records here was to conceal that conspiracy”.

The appeal also concerns whether jurors should have been allowed to hear testimony about supposed White House conversations, workflow and even Trump social media posts during his first term. His lawyers cite presidential immunity for official acts, and they argue his official conduct included responding to the Daniels drama once it became public in 2018.

“When a president addresses the nation to defend himself from allegations of personal misconduct (as all presidents do), or discusses such communications with his aides, he is carrying out his constitutional duties and is protected by immunity,” Giuffra wrote in a filing this October.

Manhattan district attorney Alvin Bragg’s office counters that the legal theory and jury instructions were legitimate and that the White House-related evidence was fair game. Some was public record, some was a general description of office practices, and the conversations were “unofficial conduct”, prosecutors say.
body_zh: 总统律师要求上诉法院驳回向斯托米·丹尼尔斯 (Stormy Daniels) 赔偿 13 万美元的刑事审判判决
周四，唐纳德·特朗普的法律团队继续努力推翻他 2024 年在封口费选举腐败案中的定罪。
美国总统的律师正试图说服纽约上诉法院推翻 2024 年 5 月的刑事审判判决，当时特朗普因在封口费腐败计划中伪造商业记录以影响他在 2016 年总统选举中最终获胜的所有指控而被判有罪。
陪审团同意他篡改记录，以掩盖支付 13 万美元的费用以让成人电影演员兼制片人斯托米·丹尼尔斯保持沉默后，他被判重罪。特朗普就在9月份再次在社交媒体上提到了此案。
2025 年 1 月初，他已经是第二个任期的当选总统，当时该案的法官给予特朗普无条件释放，这意味着他仍将是被定罪的重罪犯，但不会被判处监禁、罚款或其他处罚。
总统一直否认有任何不当行为，并已向州和联邦法院求助，希望能够撤销判决。预计他不会出席周四的法庭会议。
此次审判涉及丹尼尔斯在 2016 年大选前几周从特朗普当时的掮客兼律师迈克尔·科恩那里收到的费用。这笔钱一度让她对十年前与特朗普发生性关系的指控保持沉默，当时特朗普已经与梅拉尼娅·特朗普结婚，她还生下了他最小的儿子巴伦。特朗普坚称丹尼尔斯没有发生性行为。
然而，特朗普的公司在 2017 年向科恩报销了费用，并将这些付款记录为法律费用。
检察官称，这些交易都是为了让选民远离有关特朗普的不雅信息，并认为他“策划了一个阴谋”，违反了联邦竞选财务法等。
特朗普的律师辩称，只有“微弱”的证据表明他当时甚至知道科恩的交易。他的出庭律师还表示，向科恩支付的费用属于法律费用，只是为了避免让特朗普的家人难堪。
周四，一个由五名上诉法官组成的小组向检察官和特朗普的律师提出了很多问题，特别是关于辩方的论点，即检察官的法律理论是建立在被指控的州和联邦罪行的不稳定组合之上的。
曼哈顿地区检察官办公室表示，封口费的目的是让 2016 年选民远离有关特朗普的不雅信息，这违反了《联邦竞选法》(Feca)。
特朗普的律师小罗伯特·朱弗拉 (Robert Giuffra Jr) 告诉法官，州检察官无权将案件与联邦选举法挂钩。 “我们认为这是最明显的逆转理由，”他说。
检察官则反驳说，他们并不是在起诉所谓的联邦竞选财务犯罪，而是将其作为一个事实，推动了他们所说的导致虚假记录的阴谋。
“那么，您是否依靠 Feca 来证明您伪造的业务记录（指控）？”法官特洛伊·韦伯问道。
“只是部分原因，”曼哈顿助理地方检察官史蒂文·吴 (Steven Wu) 回答道，并补充道，“重要的是要表明这里伪造商业记录的目的是为了掩盖这一阴谋”。
该上诉还涉及陪审员是否应该被允许听取关于所谓的白宫对话、工作流程甚至特朗普在第一个任期期间社交媒体帖子的证词。他的律师援引总统对官方行为的豁免权，他们认为他的官方行为包括在丹尼尔斯的戏剧于 2018 年公开后对其做出回应。
朱弗拉在今年 10 月提交的一份文件中写道：“当一位总统向全国发表讲话，为自己免受个人不当行为的指控辩护时（就像所有总统所做的那样），或与他的助手讨论此类沟通时，他正在履行宪法职责，并受到豁免权的保护。”
曼哈顿地区检察官阿尔文·布拉格办公室反驳说，法律理论和陪审团指示是合法的，与白宫相关的证据是公平的。检察官表示，有些是公开记录，有些是对办公室做法的一般描述，而这些对话是“非官方行为”。

After Democrats' sweeping House and Senate victories, Democratic leaders are laying out how they plan to wield power with President Trump in the White House while Republicans are preparing for their time in the minority.
Democrats won at least 54 Senate seats after upsets in Texas , Kansas , South Carolina and more. The Alaska and Mississippi races remain unresolved.

12:39 AM Judge blocks DOJ from demanding election workers in Washington reject certain ballots

U.S. District Judge Jamal Whitehead granted a temporary restraining order blocking the Justice Department from demanding that election workers in Washington state reject ballots of voters suspected of being noncitizens. The department was also barred from threatening workers with prosecution if they don't comply.

"Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claim that Defendants have exceeded their authority, and the harm to Washington voters whose ballots are set aside on the strength of an unreliable federal list cannot be undone after the fact," Whitehead wrote in the ruling , which came in a lawsuit filed by several groups.

Prior to Election Day, the Justice Department pushed officials in multiple states to crack down on alleged voting by non-citizens. Federal prosecutors in Washington asked the state's top election official last week to set aside ballots from more than 400 people who they believe aren't citizens . State officials responded that "many of the persons on your list are United States citizens" and a "significant number" aren't registered to vote in the state.

title_en: Trump signs proclamation declaring Oval Office a national monument
title_zh: Trump signs proclamation declaring Oval Office a national monument
summary: The action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that President Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself.
summary_zh: The action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that President Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself.
body_en: President Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he says will preserve the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument, his first official action after his party was swept aside in midterm elections on Tuesday.

But the action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that Mr. Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself. Mr. Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors.
Mr. Trump, however, described the Oval Office order in expansive terms.

"It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Mr. Trump said. "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself."

It was the third day this week that the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington. On Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered defeats in key races across the country, Mr. Trump gathered reporters to see the final beam being raised during construction of his opulent ballroom project. On Monday, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to talk about his renovation of the landmark.

The proclamation, released after Mr. Trump's remarks, says that nothing in it will "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character."

It orders the Interior secretary to manage the Oval Office and requires "documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument." Mr. Trump separately said any major changes would need review from Congress, though such a requirement is not in the document's text.

"If they want to say, 'Let's not have oval anymore, let's make it square,' what happens is they have to go back to Congress and hopefully the Congress, the people in Congress, will be smart enough not to let that happen," said Mr. Trump — who notably demolished the East Wing of the White House to make room for his ballroom.
A red baseball cap with "VETO" on the front was sitting on the Resolute Desk as Mr. Trump signed the document, a not-so-subtle nod to the shifting of powers in Congress.

His effort to preserve changes at the White House comes as Democrats gear up for new scrutiny of Mr. Trump. Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent a flurry of letters Thursday to known donors to Mr. Trump's ballroom, demanding that they provide information or face "alternative measures to obtain compliance."

Since returning to the White House, Mr. Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents.

As he talked about his interior decorating decisions, Mr. Trump highlighted new chandeliers that he says were installed in the Cabinet Room to address "very bad lighting." His other additions to the Oval Office include numerous gold wall appliqués and gold-framed portraits.

Mr. Trump did not elaborate on precisely what he was hoping to prevent but suggested that the Oval Office might face some threat in the future. Mr. Trump himself has faced several lawsuits alleging that his Washington beautification projects were done without the necessary approval.
"If anybody ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me wherever I may be," Mr. Trump said, "and I'll come back here and I'll make sure it never happens."

Late Thursday, the National Capital Planning Commission gave final approval for the president's 250-foot triumphal arch, which will be constructed between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The NCPC, which acts as the federal government's planning agency for the region and is stacked with Trump allies, voted 8-4 to greenlight the project after almost 9 hours of public comments from members of Congress, veterans, architects and Washington, D.C., and Virginia residents.
However, a federal judge is weighing whether to temporarily block construction of the arch.

title_en: Pete Hegseth strikes defiant tone in face of impeachment threat
title_zh: Pete Hegseth strikes defiant tone in face of impeachment threat
summary: Many lawmakers, including some Republicans, have criticized the defense secretary over his handling of the Iran war.
summary_zh: Many lawmakers, including some Republicans, have criticized the defense secretary over his handling of the Iran war.
body_en: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday dismissed a renewed effort in the House to bring articles of impeachment against him as early as next week.

In a video on social media , Hegseth said, “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice.”

Hegseth was referring to Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who said Wednesday that he plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment when the House is back in session. Lawmakers are scheduled to return to Washington on Monday.
“It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth added. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”
In the more-than-five-minute video, Hegseth only briefly touched on the Iran war — a driving force behind the effort to impeach him, as well as GOP losses in this week’s midterm elections.
Massie, who lost his GOP primary after he crossed Trump, urged Trump on Thursday to replace Hegseth while he still has a GOP majority in the Senate.
“My Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress. They’ll have hearings & trials,” he said on X .
“There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns,” Massie wrote Wednesday .
Numerous Democrats have indicated a desire to oust Hegseth since their midterm election wins, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York , who is poised to be the next speaker.

Trump said Wednesday that he is not planning to replace Hegseth, and he said Thursday that Hegseth “has done a fantastic job” and “probably has opposition” over the actions he has taken, including purging military leadership.

Trump has told some allies he is considering replacing Hegseth, asking them who they think should succeed him, two people familiar with discussions told NBC News this week. He has previously insisted that he was not considering dismissing department heads just days before they were shown the door.
Massie tried to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth in September, but his efforts were stunted when House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., sent the House home early.
He would need several Republicans to join all Democrats in supporting the impeachment measure for it to succeed.

The House has impeached only two Cabinet officials in history — former President Joe Biden’s homeland security secretary, Alejandro Mayorkas, in a partisan vote, and William Belknap, the secretary of war in the 1870s. No Cabinet members have ever been convicted by the Senate.
Raquel Coronell Uribe is a politics reporter for NBC News.

title_en: Dolly Parton estate files to dismiss lawsuit against her nephew
title_zh: Dolly Parton estate files to dismiss lawsuit against her nephew
summary: The company that manages Parton’s estate had accused her nephew of threatening to destroy her brand.
summary_zh: The company that manages Parton’s estate had accused her nephew of threatening to destroy her brand.
body_en: The company that manages Dolly Parton’s estate asked a court Thursday to dismiss its legal claims against the singer’s nephew, weeks after it accused him of threatening the icon’s legacy.

She’s Alive LLC, which manages Parton’s estate, in September filed a lawsuit and sought a restraining order against Bryan Seaver, Parton’s nephew and owner of a company that provided the security detail for the singer.
On Thursday, She’s Alive filed a motion to dismiss the civil claims against Seaver in a brief one-paragraph notice.
The request was to dismiss the case without prejudice, which means it could be refiled. It was not immediately clear whether that would be pursued or if the matter was being dropped.
Attorneys for She’s Alive and Seaver did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday evening.
Parton, the beloved country music icon, died in August at 80. She had cancer.

In late September, She’s Alive filed a lawsuit alleging that Seaver had, among other things, threatened to “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships.” She’s Alive had fired Seaver and his company in mid-September, it said in the suit.
The estate manager sought a restraining order against Seaver.
In October, the estate accused Seaver of using items to barricade his property in an attempt to avoid being served with a lawsuit.
Seaver in a court filing denied accusations that he had threatened the estate , telling the court the messages were taken out of context and were about a specific business dispute.
According to Seaver, the situation stemmed from a dispute between his security company and the company that operates Parton’s hotel and museum in downtown Nashville.
Seaver’s company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, provided security for the hotel and was owed approximately $251,000 for services rendered, an affidavit filed by Seaver said.
Joe Kottke is an assignment editor at NBC News covering breaking news across the Americas, including politics, immigration, crime and severe weather.

title_en: Alabama, Florida and Indiana carry out executions on same day
title_zh: 阿拉巴马州、佛罗里达州和印第安纳州在同一天执行死刑
summary: Unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day previously happened in 2010 Alabama, Florida and Indiana all carried out executions on Thursday in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same
summary_zh: 2010年阿拉巴马州、佛罗里达州和印第安纳州曾发生过三个州同时执行死刑的不寻常事件
body_en: Unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day previously happened in 2010
Alabama, Florida and Indiana all carried out executions on Thursday in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day.

In a record-tying 19th execution of the year, Florida executed Jesse Guardado via a three-drug lethal injection. Guardado had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton county home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing.
Hours earlier, Indiana executed a man for killing two children in a house fire in 2010. And in Alabama, a man died by injection Thursday evening for his conviction in a fatal home robbery.

The death penalty in the US has faced renewed scrutiny since the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions after she survived two massive doses of pentobarbital.

Thursday’s executions were taking place the same day California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced he would commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying that he believed “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values”.
Capital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future?

Newsom’s announcement was a sharp contrast with Florida, where outgoing Republican governor Ron DeSantis has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. His state has carried out more than half of the 34 executions so far this year in the US.
It is the second time since August that three states were set to carry out executions on a single day, although it remains unusual. Prior to this year, the last time it happened was 2010.
In Indiana on Thursday, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12.45am at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, spokesperson at the state’s department of correction.

She said he had no final words. He had acknowledged killing his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped that governor Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined.
In Alabama, Michael Taylor died by lethal injection. In 1991, when he was 19, he beat two people, aged 83 and 79, to death with a metal bar during a robbery in their home in Gadsden.
Death penalty opponents had urged Alabama’s Republican governor, Kay Ivey, to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, but she declined.

Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty said: “If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life whom it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today.”

The state went forward with plans to execute Taylor, 54, by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.

Alabama executed murderer Kenneth Smith in 2024 by nitrogen asphyxiation, in an episode that witnesses found excruciating, after previously failing to succeed in its attempt to kill him using lethal injection.
‘I’m not ready, brother’: US man to be put to death months after botched execution attempt

Meanwhile, in Indiana earlier on Thursday, lawyers failed to persuade the state governor to allow Weisheit to undergo brain scans to assess a history of head injuries and mental health problems. They had asked for a life sentence.

Weisheit’s last objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week in front of the Indiana pharmacy board, the state regulatory agency.
body_zh: 2010年曾发生过三个州同一天执行死刑的罕见事件
周四，阿拉巴马州、佛罗里达州和印第安纳州均执行了死刑，这是三个州在同一天执行死刑的不同寻常的例子。
在今年创纪录的第 19 起处决中，佛罗里达州通过三种药物注射死刑处决了杰西·瓜尔达多 (Jesse Guardado)。瓜尔达多承认自己于 2004 年在沃尔顿县的家中刺死了一名 75 岁的妇女，然后偷走了她的珠宝盒、80 美元和其他贵重物品来购买毒品。这位女士帮助他找到了工作和住房。
几个小时前，印第安纳州处决了一名在 2010 年房屋火灾中杀死两名儿童的男子。在阿拉巴马州，周四晚间，一名男子因犯有致命的入室抢劫罪被注射死亡。
自从9月份田纳西州克里斯塔·派克(Christa Pike)处决失败以来，美国的死刑面临着新的审查，尽管在她两次服用大量戊巴比妥后幸存下来，法院拒绝了停止其他处决的努力。
周四执行死刑的同一天，加州州长加文·纽瑟姆 (Gavin Newsom) 宣布，他将对该州所有 548 名死刑犯进行减刑，并表示他认为“国家批准的杀戮与加州的价值观不相容”。
美国死刑数量激增——但在克里斯塔·派克被处决失败后，死刑的未来是什么？
纽瑟姆的声明与佛罗里达州形成鲜明对比，佛罗里达州即将卸任的共和党州长罗恩·德桑蒂斯像其他州长一样积极使用死刑。今年迄今为止，美国执行了 34 起处决，其中一半以上是由他所在的州执行的。
这是自八月以来第二次三个州在一天内执行死刑，尽管这仍然不寻常。今年之前，上一次发生这种情况是在2010年。
印第安纳州惩教部门发言人诺埃尔·拉塞尔 (Noelle Russell) 表示，周四上午 12 点 45 分，50 岁的杰弗里·威谢特 (Jeffrey Weisheit) 在印第安纳州密歇根城的州立监狱被宣布死亡。
她说他没有最后的话。他承认2010年在埃文斯维尔地区的一场房屋火灾中杀死了女友的两个孩子，但他希望州长迈克·布劳恩能够宽大处理，将他的刑期改为终身监禁。布劳恩拒绝了。
在阿拉巴马州，迈克尔·泰勒被注射死刑。 1991年，19岁的他在加兹登的家中遭遇抢劫，用金属棒将两名年龄分别为83岁和79岁的人打死。
死刑反对者曾敦促阿拉巴马州共和党州长凯·艾维将泰勒的刑期减至终身监​​禁，但她拒绝了。
废除死刑希望计划的埃丝特·布朗说：“如果国家杀死了迈克尔，那么杀死他的并不是那个犯下一生中最严重错误的19岁年轻人。而是今天坐在牢房里的那个成熟、受人尊敬、敬畏上帝的人。”
The state went forward with plans to execute Taylor, 54, by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional.他的律师反对在最后一刻改用注射死刑，因为他几年前选择了氮气作为死刑方法，但法官做出了对泰勒不利的裁决。
阿拉巴马州于 2024 年用氮气窒息法处决了凶手肯尼思·史密斯，这一事件令目击者感到十分痛苦，此前该州曾尝试使用注射死刑，但未能成功。

与此同时，周四早些时候在印第安纳州，律师未能说服州长允许威谢特接受脑部扫描，以评估头部受伤史和心理健康问题。他们要求判处无期徒刑。
威谢特的最后一个反对意见集中在该州计划使用从一家药房购买的致命药物，该药房下周将在印第安纳州药房委员会（州监管机构）面前举行纪律听证会。

summary: All of these seats were in districts redrawn in 2023 to favor Republican candidates.
summary_zh: 所有这些席位均位于 2023 年重新划定的选区，以支持共和党候选人。
body_en: North Carolina Democrats flipped House seats in historically GOP districts : NPR
North Carolina Democrats flipped House seats in historically GOP districts All of these seats were in districts redrawn in 2023 to favor Republican candidates.
Supporters watch Democratic senatorial candidate Roy Cooper speak during an election night event in Raleigh, N.C. on November 3, 2026. A.M STEWART/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The Associated Press has called five U.S. House races in North Carolina for Democrats, all of them in districts drawn to favor Republican candidates.
Of those districts, four are flipping from Republican control.

As of Thursday, the AP had called nine of the state's 14 House seats for Democrats and none for Republicans. It's a startling result for a delegation that went into Tuesday with 10 Republicans and four Democrats.
Here are North Carolina's 2026 election results
Races called Thursday that flipped from Republican to Democratic control included
High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson over first-term incumbent Rep. Addison McDowell in the Triad's 6th Congressional District.
Former West Virginia State Senator Richard Ojeda over National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Rep. Richard Hudson in the 9th Congressional District.
Paul Barringer over first-term incumbent Rep. Brad Knott in the 13th Congressional District, which wraps around the Raleigh exurbs.
LaKesha Womack over first-term incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, who previously served as speaker of the N.C. House of Representatives, in the 14th Congressional District.

North Carolina's Congressional map was redrawn in 2023 to significantly favor Republican candidates, and these four districts performed that way in 2024. The 14th District was the closest in that election, with Moore winning by about 16%, while the 6th District was the least competitive, with McDowell winning by more than 38%.
One of the candidates vying to replace Hudson as NRCC chair is U.S. Rep. Brian Jack, a Georgia Republican.

He wrote in a letter to fellow House Republicans that fellow GOP lawmakers may have contributed to the challenging environment. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, won the race for North Carolina's open U.S. Senate seat by nearly 20%.
What the blue wave looked like in North Carolina
"When Senate Republicans withdrew support from North Carolina weeks ago, they created a cascade that likely swept away many of our colleagues from that state," Jack wrote.
The AP also called northeastern North Carolina's 1st Congressional District for incumbent Democrat Rep. Don Davis on Thursday.

That's a district legislative Republicans redrew last year in an effort to make it easier for GOP candidates to win there, pulling Republican-leaning counties from the state's 3rd Congressional District to do so.

保罗·巴林杰 (Paul Barringer) 在第 13 国会选区（围绕罗利郊区）击败了第一任众议员布拉德·诺特 (Brad Knott)。

北卡罗来纳州国会地图于 2023 年重新绘制，明显有利于共和党候选人，而这四个选区在 2024 年的表现也是如此。在那次选举中，第 14 选区最为接近，摩尔获胜约 16%，而第 6 选区竞争力最差，麦克道尔获胜超过 38%。
竞争取代哈德森担任 NRCC 主席的候选人之一是美国佐治亚州共和党众议员布莱恩·杰克 (Brian Jack)。
