title_en: What the blue wave looked like in North Carolina
title_zh: 北卡罗来纳州的蓝浪是什么样子
summary: Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats in North Carolina. The surprising results were just one part of the blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times.
summary_zh: 民主党在北卡罗来纳州推翻了共和党控制的五个国会席位。这些令人惊讶的结果只是瑞士蓝色浪潮的一部分
body_en: What the blue wave looked like in North Carolina Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats in North Carolina. The surprising results were just one part of the blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times.
Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats in North Carolina. The surprising results were just one part of the blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times.

To North Carolina now, where Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats. That's according to race calls by The Associated Press. Democrats also held on to a redistricted seat. Most of those races, they were not even considered competitive going into Tuesday's election. The remaining congressional races in the state are still too close to call. The surprising results were just one part of the big blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times. Colin Campbell covers politics for member station WUNC. He's on the line from Raleigh. Hey there, Colin.
KELLY: OK, tell me more about North Carolina's congressional map.

CAMPBELL: So Republicans currently hold 10 of the state's 14 House seats, and last year, state lawmakers gerrymandered those maps even more to try to unseat Democrat Don Davis in the state's northeastern corner. That didn't actually happen. AP called that race for Davis today. It was one of the most expensive races in the country and one we'd all been watching along with the western North Carolina district where Democrat Jamie Ager flipped an open GOP seat by a pretty big margin.

But most of us weren't paying close attention at all to the nine districts with Republican incumbents on the ballot. All of them won by big margins two years ago, but we learned today that Congressman Tim Moore, Richard Hudson, Brad Knott and Addison McDowell all lost their seats to little-known Democrats. Hudson's particularly notable because he's actually the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. That's the campaign operation for the House GOP.
KELLY: And then there are four other Republican incumbents in North Carolina's delegation. Where do things stand for them?

CAMPBELL: None of their races have been called just yet. Three have narrow leads, but the state is still in the process of counting provisional and absentee ballots, so those numbers could change. Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx is currently just 99 votes behind her Democratic opponent. She's been in office since 2005, also chairs the House Rules Committee. All four of those races could be headed to recounts, and under our state law here, that process won't actually start until after November 13.

KELLY: So next week. So, you know, the question we've been asking for a couple of days now has been - how did Republicans manage to do so poorly? We're asking that in a lot of states. My question to you - how did Republicans do so poorly in a state where they had effectively drawn the map to favor their party?

CAMPBELL: A lot of it is the national environment. They just weren't expecting this big of a wave when they drew these maps and tried to figure out the optimal number. But North Carolina's U.S. Senate race also played a role. Former Governor Roy Cooper had such a big polling lead in that race that national Republican groups pulled all of their advertising for their candidate, Michael Whatley, moved that money to other states like Kansas in the final weeks. Most of the other Republicans here were actually relying on that spending to drive voter turnout in their races, and some of the congressional incumbents started running their own TV ads just in the final weeks of the campaign but looks like that was too little too late. Whatley ended up with less than 40% of the vote. He was Trump's pick to run for the seat but never really won over the Republican base here.
KELLY: Other things we should know about how the Blue wave broke there in North Carolina?

CAMPBELL: Democrats here easily won the state for the state Supreme Court, and they won a majority in the state House for the first time since 2008. They're pretty close to a tie in the state Senate too, which, if that happens, would be broken by the lieutenant governor who happens to be a Democrat. That's going to give Democratic Governor Josh Stein a lot more power next year, and he wants to make some redistricting reforms. Republicans, of course, still have some influence. So yesterday, he called on the two parties to come together and work on the affordability issues that dominated the election.

JOSH STEIN: What the voters want us to do is listen to what happened last night and focus on that. They want us to work for them and not be focused on reflecting pools or ballrooms or triumphal arches. They want a government that is worrying about their lives, the fact that gas has shot through the roof in price, that electricity bills are going up.
KELLY: All right, Democratic Governor Josh Stein in that reporting there from Colin Campbell, who covers North Carolina politics for member station WUNC. Thank you, Colin.

title_en: How Abdul El-Sayed actually did with Jewish voters
title_zh: 阿卜杜勒·赛义德实际上是如何对待犹太选民的
summary: Yes, he ran behind. In an interview, the senator-elect acknowledged Israel was a source of disagreement, but said he’s not changing his position.
summary_zh: 是的，他跑到了后面。在接受采访时，当选参议员承认以色列是分歧的根源，但表示他不会改变立场。
body_en: Abdul El-Sayed ran well behind other Michigan Democrats in places with more Jewish voters, according to a detailed POLITICO analysis of precinct-level results.

Statewide, the progressive senator-elect only ran two points behind Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson, getting 52.5% of the vote compared to her 54.5%. But the gap was much larger in heavily Jewish communities: In Huntington Woods, a Detroit suburb that is roughly two-thirds Jewish, El-Sayed ran nearly 15 points behind Benson, getting 65.3% of the vote compared to Benson’s 80%.
In West Bloomfield, the site of the March synagogue attack that shook the Senate primary and a town where roughly a quarter of residents are Jewish, El-Sayed ran 8.8 points behind Benson.

El-Sayed faced blowback from some Jewish Democrats during his campaign, particularly over his calls to end U.S. military support to Israel and his remarks after the synagogue attack that “hurt people hurt people,” for which he later apologized .
El-Sayed, who will be the first Muslim senator in U.S. history, told POLITICO on Wednesday that he hoped he could “earn support” from Jewish voters who hadn’t backed him in this election.

“One of the big issues of disagreement that kept showing up when it came to the Jewish community was my position on Israel,” El-Sayed said. “I'm not going to change my position, but …I intend to lead on all the issues that we agree on — whether it's the right to a union or the right to health care, clean air, clean water, or religious pluralism, and respect for the Constitution — and I hope that over time I can earn [their] support on those issues.”

El-Sayed had worked to make inroads with Jewish voters over the course of his campaign, pledging to stand up to antisemitism and for Jewish safety. Still, some Jewish leaders and activists in the state urged voters to blank their ballots in the Senate race, or back Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers.

His former Democratic primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, also switched her endorsement from El-Sayed to Rogers days before the election, citing concerns over antisemitism and the Democrat and his allies’ views and rhetoric around Israel. She pointed to an ad put out by a prominent El-Sayed supporter tying high grocery prices to U.S. aid to Israel, which El-Sayed and his campaign distanced themselves from.

Jewish voters, who make up roughly 1.4% of the Michigan electorate, have historically backed Democrats by large margins. But disagreements over support for Israel and how the party should respond to rising antisemitism are testing that voting bloc — both in Michigan and across the country.
A poll of Jewish early voters in the state found that a majority still backed El-Sayed, but roughly one in four who had supported Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024 switched to back Rogers.

With Michigan in Democrats’ early primary window for 2028, El-Sayed said his statewide win showed voters were aligned with his positioning on Israel — and that he hopes the next presidential nominee takes note.

“If you want to be where the voters are, if you want to be on the side of peace and on the side of justice and transparency, I believe that that is around holding Israel accountable to its war crimes and on making sure our tax dollars get used to do good things here rather than bad things somewhere else,” he said.

In a post-election memo , El-Sayed’s campaign touted an outside analysis finding that he only ran slightly behind Slotkin’s 2024 performance in predominantly Jewish precincts. The memo also noted he was outspent heavily in both the primary and general elections, including by “MAGA billionaires, AIPAC, Elon Musk, and corporate interests determined to elect candidates who would defend the status quo.”

But he won in a blue wave while Slotkin, who is Jewish, overcame a tough year. El-Sayed’s margins were far better than Slotkin’s numbers across nearly all of the state, suggesting Jewish voters moved in the opposite direction of most Michiganders.

On the other hand, El-Sayed particularly surged in areas with more Muslim voters, who make up roughly 2.4% of Michigan’s electorate. In Dearborn, for example, he won 82.5% of the vote compared to 78.7% for Benson. Two years ago, Slotkin won 41.4% in the city while former Vice President Kamala Harris received just 36.3% of the vote.

Lansing Mayor Andy Schor, a Jewish Democrat who supported Stevens in the primary and did not endorse El-Sayed, said he was unsurprised by that split screen. He expressed hope about El-Sayed’s relationship with the Jewish community going forward, but also said Jewish leaders should continue to raise their concerns to the incoming senator.
“Everybody has to keep talking to him. His views aren’t going to change, and we know what they are,” Schor said. But, “I hope he’s open to hearing the concerns of some of his constituents.”

Nonnegotiable Michigan, a group of Jewish activists that pushed El-Sayed on issues of Jewish safety and Israel, also said in a postelection statement that it was “prepared to work with” El-Sayed “even as we continue to hold elected leaders accountable when antisemitism enters our politics or political discourse.”
El-Sayed made clear he has no plans to change his views on Israel, but said he will be straight with voters — and that he’ll “show up for you when you need me” regardless of their differences.

“With me, what you see is what you get. And I've never once gone and told somebody that I was anything but what I am,” El-Sayed said Wednesday. “We're going to disagree. I'm going to be honest, specific and direct. And over time, I hope that I can earn support for leading on the issues on which I hope to lead and [by] serving everybody.”
body_zh: 根据《政治》杂志对选区一级结果的详细分析，阿卜杜勒·赛义德在犹太选民较多的地方远远落后于其他密歇根州民主党人。
在全州范围内，这位进步派当选参议员仅落后民主党州长当选人乔斯林·本森 (Jocelyn Benson) 两分，她获得了 52.5% 的选票，而她的得票率为 54.5%。但在犹太人口较多的社区，这种差距要大得多：在大约三分之二是犹太人的底特律郊区亨廷顿伍兹，埃尔-赛义德落后本森近 15 个百分点，获得了 65.3% 的选票，而本森只有 80%。
在西布卢姆菲尔德，三月犹太教堂袭击事件震惊了参议院初选，该镇约有四分之一的居民是犹太人，埃尔-赛义德的支持率落后本森 8.8 个百分点。
埃尔赛义德在竞选期间遭到了一些犹太民主党人的反击，特别是他呼吁结束美国对以色列的军事支持，以及他在犹太教堂袭击后发表的“伤人伤人”的言论，他后来为此道歉。
埃尔-赛义德将成为美国历史上第一位穆斯林参议员，他周三告诉《政治》杂志，他希望自己能够“赢得”在这次选举中不支持他的犹太选民的支持。
“当谈到犹太社区时，不断出现的重大分歧问题之一是我对以色列的立场，”埃尔赛义德说。 “我不会改变我的立场，但是……我打算在我们同意的所有问题上发挥领导作用——无论是工会权还是医疗保健权、清洁空气、清洁水或宗教多元化，以及尊重宪法——我希望随着时间的推移，我能够在这些问题上赢得[他们]的支持。”
埃尔-赛义德在竞选过程中一直努力争取犹太选民的支持，承诺抵制反犹太主义并维护犹太人的安全。尽管如此，该州的一些犹太领袖和活动人士仍敦促选民在参议院竞选中留白选票，或支持共和党前众议员迈克·罗杰斯。
他的前民主党主要竞争对手、众议员海莉·史蒂文斯也在选举前几天将她的支持从埃尔·赛义德转为罗杰斯，理由是对反犹太主义以及民主党及其盟友围绕以色列的观点和言论的担忧。她指出，一位著名的赛义德支持者发布的一则广告将高杂货价格与美国对以色列的援助挂钩，赛义德和他的竞选团队与此保持距离。
犹太选民约占密歇根州选民的 1.4%，历来以大幅优势支持民主党。但在支持以色列以及该党应如何应对日益高涨的反犹太主义方面存在的分歧正在考验这个投票集团——无论是在密歇根州还是在全国各地。
对该州犹太早期选民的一项民意调查发现，大多数人仍然支持埃尔-赛义德，但大约四分之一的 2024 年支持参议员埃丽莎·斯洛特金的人转而支持罗杰斯。
密歇根州正处于民主党 2028 年的早期初选窗口，埃尔-赛义德表示，他在全州范围内的胜利表明选民与他对以色列的立场一致，他希望下一任总统候选人能够注意到这一点。
他说：“如果你想站在选民的立场上，如果你想站在和平一边，站在正义和透明一边，我认为那就是让以色列对其战争罪行负责，并确保我们的税款在这里用来做好事，而不是在其他地方做坏事。”
在一份选举后的备忘录中，埃尔·赛义德的竞选团队吹捧了一项外部分析结果，该分析发现，他在 2024 年在犹太人占主导地位的选区的表现仅略落后于斯洛特金。备忘录还指出，他在初选和大选中的支出都超过了他，其中包括“MAGA 亿万富翁、AIPAC、埃隆·马斯克和决心选举捍卫现状的候选人的企业利益集团”。
但他在蓝色浪潮中获胜，而犹太人斯洛特金则克服了艰难的一年。在几乎全州范围内，埃尔-赛义德的支持率远高于斯洛特金的支持率，这表明犹太选民的投票方向与大多数密歇根人相反。
另一方面，埃尔-赛义德在穆斯林选民较多的地区尤其飙升，穆斯林选民约占密歇根州选民的 2.4%。例如，在迪尔伯恩，他赢得了 82.5% 的选票，而本森赢得了 78.7% 的选票。两年前，斯洛特金在该市赢得了 41.4% 的选票，而前副总统卡马拉·哈里斯 (Kamala Harris) 仅获得 36.3% 的选票。
兰辛市市长安迪·肖尔（Andy Schor）是一名犹太民主党人，他在初选中支持史蒂文斯，但不支持埃尔·赛义德。他表示，他对分屏并不感到惊讶。他对埃尔赛义德与犹太社区的关系未来发展表示希望，但也表示犹太领导人应继续向即将上任的参议员提出他们的担忧。
“每个人都必须继续与他交谈。他的观点不会改变，我们知道这些观点是什么，”肖尔说。但是，“我希望他愿意倾听一些选民的担忧。”
不可谈判的密歇根州是一个在犹太安全和以色列问题上推动埃尔赛义德的犹太活动家组织，该组织也在一份选举后声明中表示，它“准备与”埃尔赛义德合作，“即使当反犹太主义进入我们的政治或政治话语时，我们仍将继续追究民选领导人的责任”。
埃尔-赛义德明确表示，他不打算改变对以色列的看法，但表示他将坦诚地对待选民，并且无论选民之间存在分歧，他都会“在你们需要我的时候出现在你们身边”。
“对我来说，所见即所得。我从来没有告诉过别人我不是我，”埃尔-赛义德周三说道。 “我们会不同意。我会诚实、具体和直接。随着时间的推移，我希望我能够赢得支持，以领导我希望领导和服务所有人的问题。”

title_en: Newsom announces he will commute sentences of inmates on California's death row
title_zh: 纽森宣布将为加州死囚减刑
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row. The governor says at 548 people, it's the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
summary_zh: 加州州长加文·纽瑟姆宣布，他将对该州死囚区的所有囚犯进行减刑。州长说有 548 人，
body_en: Newsom announces he will commute sentences of inmates on California's death row California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row. The governor says at 548 people, it's the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row. The governor says at 548 people, it's the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.

California Governor Gavin Newsom announced today that he is commuting all 548 death sentences on the books in his state. He is reducing all of the sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The governor says California's death row is the largest in the Western hemisphere. Now, this action comes during a renewed national debate about capital punishment, following the recent botched execution attempt of a woman convicted of murder in Tennessee and also following the Trump administration's talk of livestreaming an execution at Fort Hood. That proposal was later rejected by President Trump. Scott Shafer of member station KQED is following the California governor's action today and joins us now. Hi, Scott.
CHANG: OK, so how did Governor Newsom explain his reasons for taking this step?

SHAFER: Well, the governor has been thinking about this for a long time now. He signaled on his podcast last month that he was framing it as a rocking chair test, meaning - how would he feel when he's old and sitting in a rocking chair reflecting on his life? He clearly sees opposition to the death penalty as, you know, kind of fundamental to his values and his faith. So it was pretty clear this was going to happen. They waited until just after the election to do it. He issued a statement today explaining why he did this, and among other things, he said the death penalty is a failure. You know, we haven't had an execution in California in 20 years. He also said it's immoral for the state to murder somebody and that it isn't applied fairly anyway.
CHANG: OK. Well, Newsom had already put death sentences on hold, right? So explain how this step today differs from that earlier step.

SHAFER: Yeah, he issued that moratorium on executions two months after he became governor - that was 2019 - dismantled the execution chamber at San Quentin prison, and they moved death row inmates from San Quentin to other maximum-security prisons across the state. So in some ways, this is symbolic since there aren't any executions on the horizon anyway. But by commuting these hundreds of sentences, it might give momentum to death penalty opponents in other states, you know, to lobby governors there to do something similar. And I should emphasize, Ailsa, that Newsom's actions today do not eliminate the death penalty in California. Only the voters can do that.
CHANG: Right. OK, so what's been the reaction so far there in California? Like, what have victims had to say about this?

SHAFER: Well, Newsom met with many crime victims before he issued the moratorium on executions back in 2019. Needless to say, those are very hard conversations, very raw. He met with many of those folks again over the past months as he considered this decision, and in his statement today, he sort of spoke to them saying, commuting these death sentences could resurface excruciating memories for them. He does not dismiss that in any way. He also said that he didn't want to pick and choose which death sentences to commute and which to let stand, saying that that could inadvertently create two classes of murder victims, which he did not want to do.

CHANG: OK. Well, you suggest that today's actions by Newsom were pretty anticipated. I mean, Newsom is often mentioned as a possible candidate for president in 2028. So talk about the political context here for this move.

SHAFER: Yeah, this was anticipated, for those of us paying attention to it. He waited until after Tuesday's election, so it wouldn't become an issue. And as to the politics, you know, there are certainly some advisers in Newsom's political orbit who urged him not to do it as he gets ready to run for president. But one of his advisers said that when he did this seven years ago, Newsom never asked to see any polls or look at anything related to the politics of it. And across the country, Gallup has been polling on this for decades, and support for the death penalty is at its lowest point in decades. So it's not really clear Newsom will pay a political price for this.
CHANG: That is Scott Shafer from member station KQED in San Francisco. Thank you, Scott.

title_en: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman wins Los Angeles mayoral race over incumbent Karen Bass

summary: Major shake-up as LA councilmember, once considered long shot, ousts Democratic rival she had once endorsed Who is Nithya Raman, Los Angeles’s next mayor? Nithya Raman was elected to serve as the mayor of Los Angeles, defeating incumbent Karen Bass in a major
summary_zh: 曾经被认为可能性不大的洛杉矶市议员，驱逐了她曾经支持的民主党竞争对手，发生了重大改组。 谁是洛杉矶的下一届市长 Nithya Raman
body_en: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman wins Los Angeles mayoral race over incumbent Karen Bass | US midterm elections 2026
Major shake-up as LA councilmember, once considered long shot, ousts Democratic rival she had once endorsed
Who is Nithya Raman, Los Angeles’s next mayor?
Nithya Raman was elected to serve as the mayor of Los Angeles , defeating incumbent Karen Bass in a major political shake-up that reflects the growing dissatisfaction with the direction of the city.

The progressive urban planner had served on LA’s city council since 2020. She caused a stir when she entered the race earlier this year hours before the filing deadline – and shortly after endorsing Bass for re-election – and her campaign was once viewed as a long shot.
US midterm elections 2026: live results from Senate, House and governor races in all 50 states

But she shot up in the polls over the summer and, with support from the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, frequently garnered comparisons with Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor.
The Associated Press called the race for Raman on Thursday, with returns showing Raman was leading with just over 52% of the votes to Bass’s 48%.

Raman’s win came after a historic election night for Democrats across the US who won control of the House and Senate in a rebuke of Donald Trump and his party. The contest in deep blue Los Angeles was unique by comparison. Raman and Bass are progressives, and the mayoral race became a bitter battle between two candidates representing different generations and frequently clashing wings of the party.
“I love this city and I love its people. And I cannot wait to get started on building a better future together with all of you,” Raman said in a video statement after her victory.
Raman also heaped praise on her former ally Bass, describing her “someone who has given decades of her life to making the city what it is today”.
The conciliatory tone marked a departure from a contentious race, where Raman and Bass traded biting remarks about each other’s perceived failures to address the city’s woes.

Bass had never before lost an election, but faced a difficult road to winning another term as mayor given her low approval ratings on par with Donald Trump’s, Angelenos’ frustration about the state of the city, and the wave of anti-establishment sentiment that has swept US politics .
The election came as Los Angeles grappled with significant challenges, including frustration over homelessness, as well as rising costs and housing affordability.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration’s deportation campaign hit the region hard, Hollywood is struggling, and the city faces a huge budget shortfall.

“While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,” Bass said on Thursday. “I have called councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”
Raman pitched herself to voters as the candidate who can “meet this moment with honesty and urgency” while lowering rents, improving city streets, reducing homelessness and keeping Angelenos safe.
She struggled in the primary – key portions of the city’s liberal base and large unions had already aligned with Bass – and was overshadowed by Spencer Pratt’s showy campaign.

Pratt, a former reality TV star and registered Republican, decided to run after he lost his home in the Palisades fire. He had splashy and viral campaign ads critical of the mayor and Raman. He was a frequent thorn in Bass’s side, arguing she was mismanaging the city, and that officials had both failed to adequately prepare for the fire and were falling short in recovery efforts.
body_zh: 民主社会主义者尼西亚·拉曼 (Nithya Raman) 击败现任凯伦·巴斯 (Karen Bass) 赢得洛杉矶市长竞选2026 年美国中期选举
曾经被认为可能性不大的洛杉矶市议员推翻了她曾经支持的民主党竞争对手，发生了重大改组
洛杉矶下一任市长 Nithya Raman 是谁？
尼西亚·拉曼（Nithya Raman）在一场重大政治变动中击败现任洛杉矶市长凯伦·巴斯（Karen Bass）当选洛杉矶市长，这反映出人们对这座城市的发展方向日益不满。
这位进步的城市规划师自 2020 年以来一直在洛杉矶市议会任职。今年早些时候，她在提交截止日期前几小时参加竞选，当时她在支持巴斯连任后不久，引起了轰动，她的竞选曾被视为希望渺茫。
2026 年美国中期选举：所有 50 个州参议院、众议院和州长竞选的实时结果
但今年夏天，她在民意调查中的支持率飙升，并且在美国民主社会主义者洛杉矶分会的支持下，经常被拿来与纽约市市长佐兰·马姆达尼进行比较。
美联社周四宣布了拉曼的竞选，结果显示拉曼以略高于 52% 的得票率领先巴斯，得票率为 48%。
拉曼的胜利是在美国各地的民主党人经历了历史性的选举之夜之后发生的，他们在唐纳德·特朗普及其政党的谴责中赢得了众议院和参议院的控制权。相比之下，在深蓝色洛杉矶举行的比赛是独一无二的。拉曼和巴斯都是进步派人士，市长竞选成为两位代表不同世代、党内两翼经常发生冲突的候选人之间的一场苦战。
“我爱这座城市，我爱它的人民。我迫不及待地想开始与你们所有人一起建设更美好的未来，”拉曼在获胜后的视频声明中说道。
拉曼还对她的前盟友巴斯大加赞扬，称她是“一个奉献了数十年生命的人，才让这座城市成为今天的样子”。
这种和解的语气标志着一场有争议的竞选的背离，当时拉曼和巴斯就彼此认为未能解决该市困境的问题交换了尖锐的言论。
巴斯以前从未输过一次选举，但由于她的支持率与唐纳德·特朗普相当，洛杉矶人对城市状况感到沮丧，以及席卷美国政坛的反建制情绪浪潮，她在连任市长时面临着一条艰难的道路。
此次选举之际，洛杉矶正在应对重大挑战，包括对无家可归者的不满，以及不断上升的成本和住房负担能力。
与此同时，特朗普政府的驱逐行动对该地区造成了沉重打击，好莱坞陷入困境，该市面临巨大的预算缺口。
“虽然这不是我们希望的结果，但洛杉矶人民已经发声了，”巴斯周四表示。 “我已致电市议员尼西亚·拉曼（Nithya Raman）祝贺她的胜利，我已承诺确保顺利、无缝的过渡。推动这座城市向前发展是洛杉矶需要我们所有人做的事情。”
拉曼向选民推销自己，称自己是一位能够“诚实而紧迫地迎接这一时刻”的候选人，同时降低租金、改善城市街道、减少无家可归者并确保洛杉矶人的安全。
她在初选中举步维艰——该市自由派基础的关键部分和大型工会已经与巴斯结盟——并被斯宾塞·普拉特华丽的竞选活动所掩盖。
普拉特是一位前真人秀明星，也是注册共和党人，他在帕利塞兹火灾中失去了家园后决定参选。他制作了引人注目且病毒式传播的竞选广告，批评市长和拉曼。他经常成为巴斯的眼中钉，认为她对这座城市的管理不善，而且官员们既没有为火灾做好充分的准备，也没有在恢复工作方面做得不够。

title_en: US holds secret talks with Tehran to deport Iranians even as war drags on, court documents show
title_zh: 法庭文件显示，即使战争仍在继续，美国仍与德黑兰举行秘密会谈，以驱逐伊朗人
summary: Trump administration push emerges from a lawsuit alleging violations of national immigration regulations The Trump administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by the Associated Pre
summary_zh: 特朗普政府的推动源于一项指控违反国家移民法规的诉讼 特朗普政府与特朗普政府举行了秘密会谈
body_en: Trump administration push emerges from a lawsuit alleging violations of national immigration regulations
The Trump administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by the Associated Press show.

The court documents unsealed on Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so.

The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days’ written notice before any such deportation is carried out.

“We are at war with a country where the president of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless … A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors,” the judge, Ana Reyes, said according to the 15 October transcript that has now been unsealed.

“And what you’re telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death.”
“Yes, your honor,” justice department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. “The government is executing lawful orders of removal.”

Georgiev-Remmel told the court there was no specific date set to carry out any removals. A legal group representing Iranians held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) said a dozen Iranian detainees had been given notice over the past week that they would be deported to Iran. The legal group, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, brought the lawsuit in which the transcript was released.

The court documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out “possible avenues for removal”.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE’s parent agency , and the state department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The development emerged from an ongoing lawsuit that alleges the Trump administration’s immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings argue.

The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said on Thursday at least 12 Iranian detainees have been contacted by the Iranian Interest Section, an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs, in the past week and notified of an upcoming deportation flight to Iran through Pakistan. The group did not say when the deportation would occur.

One of those detainees attempted suicide once he learned he might be returned to Iran, according to Yasmine Chubin, the executive director of the organization. He was one of two people who were subsequently moved across state lines to a detention center in Texas, where detainees are often relocated immediately preceding a removal.
None of the detainees who have been contacted have been provided any information in writing from immigration authorities, the legal group said.
Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent.

The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the US and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in ICE custody and pressure them to return to Iran – a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments. The DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government.

Hundreds of emails exchanged between US immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026.

During the 15 October hearing, Reyes warned government attorneys that she would initiate contempt proceedings if the administration violated her order to give the court advance notice of any planned deportation flights.
“We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country,” Reyes said.
body_zh: 特朗普政府的推动源于一项指控违反国家移民法规的诉讼
美联社获得的法庭文件显示，特朗普政府与伊朗就驱逐伊朗人问题进行了秘密会谈，尽管那里的战争仍在拖延。
周四公布的法庭文件显示，共和党政府最近在 10 月中旬表示，计划通过未透露姓名的第三国驱逐伊朗人，但尚不清楚其打算何时这样做。
该案法官命令政府就任何将伊朗人驱逐到伊朗或任何其他国家的最终计划提前 24 小时通知法院，并在执行任何此类驱逐之前提前五天书面通知。
根据现已启封的 10 月 15 日笔录，法官安娜·雷耶斯 (Ana Reyes) 表示：“我们正在与一个国家交战，美国总统就在两三天前甚至昨天还曾表示，这个国家本质上是无法无天的……根据现任总统的说法，这个国家是美国的敌人。根据我们的总统的说法，这个国家谋杀了数万名抗议者。”
“你告诉我的是，美利坚合众国将把一些人送回那个地区，面对你和我以及所有关注此事的人都知道，至少会面临死亡的严重威胁。”
“是的，法官大人，”司法部律师迪米塔·格奥尔基耶夫-雷梅尔说。 “政府正在执行合法的驱逐令。”
格奥尔基耶夫-雷梅尔告诉法庭，目前还没有确定具体的搬迁日期。一个代表被移民和海关执法局（ICE）关押的伊朗人的法律团体表示，过去一周已有十几名伊朗被拘留者接到通知，称他们将被驱逐到伊朗。法律团体伊朗裔美国人法律辩护基金会提起了诉讼，并公布了诉讼记录。
法庭文件显示，政府在战争期间就驱逐事宜与伊朗官员保持着联系，特别是提交旅行证件和找出“可能的驱逐途径”。
ICE 的上级机构国土安全部 (DHS) 和国务院没有立即回应置评请求。
法庭文件称，这一进展源于一项正在进行的诉讼，该诉讼指控特朗普政府的移民机构一直与伊朗政府分享有关伊朗寻求庇护者的机密信息，违反了国家移民法规，并危及无数伊朗人。
伊朗美国法律辩护基金会周四表示，过去一周，巴基斯坦驻华盛顿大使馆负责处理领事事务的伊朗代表处伊朗利益科联系了至少 12 名伊朗被拘留者，并通知他们即将通过巴基斯坦飞往伊朗。该组织没有透露何时会进行驱逐。
该组织执行主任亚斯敏·楚宾 (Yasmine Chubin) 表示，其中一名被拘留者在得知自己可能被遣返伊朗后试图自杀。他是随后被跨州转移到德克萨斯州拘留中心的两人之一，被拘留者经常在被转移之前立即被重新安置。
该法律组织表示，所联系的被拘留者均未收到移民当局的任何书面信息。
国外的活动人士对被驱逐者返回伊朗表示担忧，伊朗的神权政治一直在打压知识分子，政府也大力镇压任何异议。
该诉讼描绘了美国和伊朗政府之间协调一致的行动，以识别被 ICE 拘留的伊朗人，并迫使他们返回伊朗 — — 这明显背离了两国政府之间数十年的外交敌对状态。国土安全部否认与伊朗政府分享庇护申请记录。
美国移民官员之间交换的数百封电子邮件揭露了两国如何合作，安排100多名伊朗人在2025年9月、2025年12月和2026年1月乘坐三趟移民航班返回伊朗。
在 10 月 15 日的听证会上，雷耶斯警告政府律师，如果政府违反她向法院提前通知任何计划的驱逐航班的命令，她将启动藐视法庭诉讼。
雷耶斯说：“我们正在讨论将我们照顾和拘留的人员送往我们轰炸过的国家，我们可能会继续轰炸，并且他们是这个国家的敌人。”

The Trump administration has escalated its economic campaign against Cuba

The Trump administration on Thursday escalated its economic campaign against Cuba , issuing a determination that clears the path for U.S. sanctions on several crucial sectors of the island's economy while also targeting Chinese-based suppliers to Havana's military forces.

The sanctions are part of a larger effort by President Donald Trump and his allies to force political change in Havana even as the country continues to grapple with a deepening economic and energy crisis that has suffocated its population.
With the new penalties the State Department is expanding its reach to target new sectors of Cuba's economy, including electronics, manufacturing, marine and technology.

“Cuba’s ruling elite is hoarding the island’s energy, shipping, and technology resources for its own enrichment, leaving the Cuban people to contend with blackouts, shortages, and a stagnant economy,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.

In total, eight entities and two individuals were targeted, including China National Electronic Import and Export Company and Beijing H & C Technologies, two China-based companies that the U.S. is accusing of procuring weapons and selling surveillance and security equipment to the Cuban government.

Voters in Washington and Colorado have approved measures to ban transgender athletes from participating in school sports
Voters in left-leaning Washington state and Colorado have approved measures designed to ban transgender athletes from participating in school-sanctioned sports.

Measure 638 in Washington, which had more than 56% of the vote, will prevent students who were assigned male at birth from participating in sports designated for female athletes. The measure also requires athletes wanting to play in female sports to produce a statement from a health care provider verifying their gender.

Proposition 134 in Colorado will require educational institutions and athletic associations to assign sports as male, female or coed. The proposal, which was supported by 52% of voters, will also limit athletes to playing in sports in the gender they were assigned at birth.
The votes came in states where Democratic-led governors’ offices and legislatures have declined to enact the kind of bans that have become the norm in Republican-led states.

Supporters of the bans decided to force the issue by putting it on the ballot, and the results indicate that what conservatives once used as a wedge issue in the culture wars has become one of the few to receive bipartisan support.

“This was always coming because politicians in those states have been ignoring their constituencies on the ground,” said Doriane Lambelet Coleman, a professor at Duke Law School. “And, as we saw on Tuesday, there’s only so long that can work. Whether other blue states join Washington and Colorado depends on local political culture and on the ability of the advocacy groups on both sides of the issue to marshal their troops.”
The passages came during the same election cycle in which Arizona voters chose to expand restrictions initially outlined in a 2022 law.

Proposition 318 will prohibit transgender girls from participating in female sports in all schools and athletic associations — they were already barred from doing so in public schools — and limit transgender people to using bathrooms and other private spaces to the gender they were assigned at birth.
The proposition also requires an athlete's “sex” to reflect what they were assigned on their birth certificate and allows athletes to sue schools and associations that violate the expanded law.

Nebraska, which already had a ban in place on transgender athletes, codified the ban in the state constitution after passing Measure 442. The measure requires schools to designate a sport as male, female or coed and prohibits students assigned male at birth from participating in female sports.

Other transgender bans have gone to the courts. A county-level ban in suburban Nassau County outside New York City was struck down by an appeals court Tuesday in a setback to the GOP nominee for governor, who championed the legislation while serving as county executive.

Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA

The results in Washington and Colorado came less than two years after President Donald Trump signed an executive order titled “Keeping Men Out of Women’s Sports,” which gave federal agencies wide latitude to ensure entities that receive federal funding abide by Title IX in alignment with the Trump administration’s view, which interprets “sex” as the gender someone was assigned at birth.

title_en: Harmeet Dhillon, controversial head of DoJ’s civil rights division, steps down
title_zh: 备受争议的司法部民权部门负责人哈米特·迪隆 (Harmeet Dhillon) 辞职

body_en: Harmeet Dhillon, controversial head of DoJ’s civil rights division, steps down | US midterm elections 2026
Dhillon is first high-level justice department official to leave after historic Republican defeat in 2026 midterms
Harmeet Dhillon, a Donald Trump ally who led the justice department’s civil rights division, is leaving her position.

“Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months. She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors,” the attorney general, Todd Blanche, said in a post on X .

Dhillon is the first high-ranking justice department official to leave after the midterm elections in which Democrats took control of Congress. Democrats are expected to use that power to aggressively investigate executive agencies, including the justice department. Dhillon’s departure was first reported by Bloomberg Law.

Dhillon dramatically transformed the civil rights division in a little over a year and a half there, reorienting its mission away from the work it had traditionally done protecting the civil rights of minorities. Under her leadership, the department dropped many cases alleging discrimination against racial minorities in voting, housing, employment and education. Scores of career lawyers also left the division under her leadership, leading to an exodus of expertise of civil rights enforcement.
Harmeet Dhillon: DoJ lawyer a top contender for Trump’s retribution mission

Dhillon aggressively pursued claims of discrimination at universities, including claims that minorities were unfairly favored in admissions and claims of antisemitism against Jewish students. A whistleblower has said that investigations into the schools were conducted with a predetermined outcome and that lawyers were told to find a reason to file a lawsuit.

The civil rights division also oversaw investigations into the killing of US citizens Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good by federal agents in Minnesota during an immigration enforcement surge – neither has resulted in criminal charges.

“From day one, Harmeet Dhillon abdicated her responsibility to enforce our nation’s federal civil rights laws and destroyed the crown jewel of the justice department,” said Kristen Clarke, who led the civil rights division under Joe Biden and is now general counsel at the NAACP.
“Instead of protecting the civil rights of all Americans, she abandoned cases, purged the work force and weaponized the division to target institutions to achieve illegitimate, partisan goals.”

The division also had some high-profile failures under Dhillon’s watch. It sued more than two dozen states for voter roll information and lost every single case. Several of the judges who ruled against the department were appointed by Donald Trump

“Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless and hateful head of the civil rights division in DoJ history,” said Stacey Young, a former civil rights division lawyer who now leads the group Justice Connection, a group for justice department alumni.

She added: “After she upended the division’s mission-critical work, the civil servants who dedicated their careers to protecting vulnerable communities were instead told to target them – and more than three-quarters of the division’s lawyers left. Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the justice department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court.”

A prolific poster on X, Dhillon would sometimes reveal civil rights investigations on the platform, a move that startled longtime justice department lawyers because the department has a longstanding practice of not speaking publicly about investigations. She has also publicly used a slur for people with disabilities, whose civil rights her division is charged with protecting. She has also described conservative influencers as “hoes” .

Dhillon grew up in Smithfield, North Carolina, after being born in India and then living in the UK and New York. “There were Klan signs on the highway where I grew up. I’m used to being an outsider. My superpower is not really caring what people think about me,” she told the Dartmouth alumni magazine last year.
Before joining the government, Dhillon ran her own law firm and was vice-chair of the California GOP. After the 2020 election, she worked on lawsuits contesting the election results.
body_zh: 备受争议的司法部民权部门负责人哈米特·迪隆 (Harmeet Dhillon) 辞职 | 2026 年美国中期选举
迪隆是共和党在 2026 年中期选举中历史性失败后第一位离职的司法部高级官员
唐纳德·特朗普的盟友、司法部民权部门负责人哈米特·迪隆 (Harmeet Dhillon) 即将离职。
“今天，我接受了助理总检察长哈米特·迪伦 (Harmeet Dhillon) 的辞职，她在过去 18 个月里以有罪的态度领导了民权部门。她捍卫了每个美国人的公民自由，并毫无畏惧或偏袒地执行法律。司法部感谢她热心的公共服务，我们祝愿她在未来的工作中一切顺利，”总检察长托德·布兰奇 (Todd Blanche) 在 X 上的帖子中说道。
迪隆是民主党控制国会的中期选举后第一位离职的司法部高级官员。预计民主党人将利用这一权力积极调查包括司法部在内的行政机构。彭博法律首先报道了迪隆离职的消息。
迪隆在一年半多的时间里对民权部门进行了戏剧性的转变，将其使命从传统上保护少数群体民权的工作中转移出来。在她的领导下，该部门撤销了许多指控少数族裔在投票、住房、就业和教育方面受到歧视的案件。数十名职业律师也离开了她领导下的部门，导致民权执法方面的专业知识外流。
哈米特·迪伦（Harmeet Dhillon）：司法部律师是特朗普报复任务的最佳竞争者
迪隆积极追究大学歧视的指控，包括少数族裔在招生中受到不公平对待的指控以及针对犹太学生的反犹太主义指控。一名举报人表示，对学校的调查是有预定结果的，律师被告知要找到提起诉讼的理由。
民权部门还监督了对明尼苏达州联邦特工在移民执法激增期间杀害美国公民亚历克斯·普雷蒂（Alex Pretti）和蕾妮·妮可·古德（Renee Nicole Good）的调查，但两人均未受到刑事指控。
“从第一天起，哈米特·迪隆就放弃了执行我们国家联邦民权法的责任，并摧毁了司法部皇冠上的明珠，”乔·拜登领导下的民权部门负责人、现任全国有色人种协进会总法律顾问克里斯汀·克拉克说。
“她没有保护所有美国人的公民权利，而是放弃了案件，清洗了劳动力，并将该部门武器化，以针对机构来实现非法的党派目标。”
在迪隆的领导下，该部门也遭遇了一些引人注目的失败。它起诉了二十多个州，要求提供选民名册信息，但每一起案件都败诉。几名做出对该部门不利裁决的法官是由唐纳德·特朗普任命的
“哈米特·迪隆是司法部历史上最具破坏性、无法无天和最可恨的民权部门负责人，”前民权部门律师史黛西·杨(Stacey Young)说，她现在领导着司法部校友组织“正义连接”(Justice Connection)。
她补充道：“在她颠覆了该部门的关键任务工作后，那些致力于保护弱势社区的公务员反而被告知要以他们为目标——该部门超过四分之三的律师离开了。迪隆利用司法部的巨大权力，在虚假案件中威胁大学、州和地方官员以及选举工作人员，而这些案件很少在法庭上获胜。”
Dhillon 是 X 上多产的发帖者，有时会在平台上揭露民权调查，这一举动令司法部的长期律师感到震惊，因为该部门长期以来一直不公开谈论调查。她还公开诽谤残疾人，而她的部门负责保护残疾人的公民权利。她还将保守派影响者描述为“锄头”。
迪伦出生于印度，后来居住在英国和纽约，之后在北卡罗来纳州的史密斯菲尔德长大。 “我长大的高速公路上有三K党的标志。我已经习惯了成为局外人。我的超能力并不真正关心人们对我的看法，”她去年告诉达特茅斯校友杂志。
在加入政府之前，迪伦经营着自己的律师事务所，并担任加州共和党副主席。 2020 年大选后，她参与了针对选举结果的诉讼。

title_en: Judge blocks construction on Trump’s D.C.-area arch after commission’s approval
title_zh: Judge blocks construction on Trump’s D.C.-area arch after commission’s approval
summary: The Trump administration has said it expects to begin construction immediately, but a judge is considering a plan to temporarily halt the project.
summary_zh: The Trump administration has said it expects to begin construction immediately, but a judge is considering a plan to temporarily halt the project.
body_en: Federal panel expected to approve Trump's 250-foot arch as backlash continues
Nov. 5, 2026, 1:56 PM EST / Updated Nov. 6, 2026, 1:57 AM EST
By Gary Grumbach , Julia Eisen , Megan Brand , Maggie McCabe and Dareh Gregorian
A federal judge late Thursday temporarily blocked construction on President Donald Trump’s “Triumphal Arch” shortly after a planning commission led by Trump appointees approved it.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan granted a temporary restraining order blocking the administration from “initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation” or other steps in the arch project for 14 days.

Chutkan’s order came within an hour of the National Capital Planning Commission’s approval of the massive and controversial arch project, which would sit in Memorial Circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The District of Columbia and Virginia, who are suing over the project, filed a motion for the temporary restraining order. In an opinion accompanying her order Chutkan said they have demonstrated a likelihood of standing to sue and an immediate harm.
Chutkan wrote in the opinion that “the harm is certain” and that the Trump administration has said it was ready to start construction almost immediately after the commission’s approval.
The commission passed the motion to approve final site building plans 8-4, with the four votes in opposition coming from commissioners who were not appointed by Trump.
Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., whose district includes the cemetery, applauded the ruling and accused Trump of trying to bypass legal barriers.

“This fight is not over. While this decision prevents Donald Trump from immediately implementing his plans to create a monument to his own ego, the courts and Congress must put in place permanent safeguards to stop the Trump Administration from violating the law and proceeding with this project,” Beyer said in a statement.
The Department of Interior and National Park Service did not immediately respond to requests for comment about Chutkan’s order early Friday.
The commission gave the project a green light after a hearing at which scores of area residents lined up to voice their opposition to the project.

Public comment at the hearing lasted more than nine hours, which commission Chair Mark Paoletta said was “more than ever.” The comments mostly related to the impact on Arlington National Cemetery, which is the final resting place of the nation’s fallen service members, as well as the project’s height, scale and safety.

Paoletta, who is general counsel at the Office of Management and Budget and was appointed chairman of the commission in August, said at the meeting that it was a “national disgrace” that such a memorial had not already been built. He also praised Trump’s “monumental vision,” saying it would be “the grandest arch ever built by mankind.”

The virtual meeting was interrupted for around 30 minutes during public comments by what Paoletta said was a “malicious attack” that caused the site to crash. He said it’s the “first time this has ever happened.”
Close to 130 members of the public were signed up to speak.
“We’ll have this thing done, whether it’s past midnight or not,” Paoletta said after the interruption. The vote ended in the 10 p.m. hour.
Reps. Brian Mast, R-Fla., and Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., spoke in favor of the project, while Beyer expressed concern over the project and criticized the Trump administration over the approval process.
The governments of Virginia and the District of Columbia have argued the project is illegal.

title_en: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
title_zh: 巴拉圭总统因银行倒闭辞职几分钟后被弹劾
summary: Paraguayan lawmakers voted to impeach President Santiago Peña minutes after his resignation, as the collapse of a digital bank tied to his government froze millions of people's savings.
summary_zh: 巴拉圭立法者在总统圣地亚哥·佩纳辞职后几分钟投票弹劾他，因为与他的政府有关的数字银行倒闭了
body_en: A demonstrator holds a mock U.S. dollar bill depicting Paraguayan President Santiago Peña during a protest against the government and Ueno Bank, which Paraguay's central bank seized amid a solvency crisis, in Asunción, Paraguay, Wednesday. Jorge Saenz/AP hide caption

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation Thursday after the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government triggered widespread protests, froze millions of people's savings and cost him the support of his own party.

The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration.

Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation later Thursday, clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial.

Opposition senators were still demanding a trial, arguing that allowing Peña to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution.
Paraguay President Santiago Peña speaks to the media at United Nations headquarters, Sept. 19, 2023. Ted Shaffrey/AP hide caption

As lawmakers debated his impeachment, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations that the Trump administration lifted last year.

Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages.
"I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."
The turmoil has hit Paraguay's currency. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the U.S. dollar Thursday, bringing its losses this week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data.

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings.
"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.
As recently as last month, Peña defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
body_zh: 周三，在巴拉圭亚松森，一名示威者在抗议政府和上野银行时举着一张描绘巴拉圭总统圣地亚哥·佩纳的模拟美元钞票。上野银行是巴拉圭央行在偿付能力危机中没收的。豪尔赫·萨恩斯/美联社隐藏标题栏
巴拉圭亚松森——周四，巴拉圭总统圣地亚哥·佩纳宣布辞职，原因是一家与巴拉圭政府相关的大型数字银行倒闭，引发了广泛的抗议活动，冻结了数百万人的储蓄，并使他失去了自己政党的支持。
上野银行的危机使佩纳长期执政的科罗拉多党对他不利，这对这位前国际货币基金组织经济学家来说是一个惊人的逆转，他曾得到该国最有权势的政客的支持，几周前作为特朗普政府的重要盟友在华盛顿受到欢迎。
佩纳宣布这一消息后几分钟，下议院以 78 比 0 的投票结果弹劾他，并将指控送交参议院。预计国会领导人将于周四晚些时候接受他的辞职，为副总统佩德罗·阿利亚纳无需等待参议院审判就宣誓就职扫清道路。
反对派参议员仍然要求进行审判，认为允许佩纳辞职将保留他终身成为参议员的资格，并提供法律保护以防止他被起诉。
巴拉圭总统圣地亚哥·佩纳于 2023 年 9 月 19 日在联合国总部向媒体发表讲话。Ted Shaffrey/美联社 隐藏标题栏
当议员们就弹劾案进行辩论时，佩纳在发布到 X 的视频中表示，他是为了“我们国家的稳定、社会和平以及维护我们民主制度的需要”而辞职。
就连佩纳的导师、科罗拉多党领袖、前总统奥拉西奥·卡特斯也支持弹劾，称该党不会支持“掠夺公共和私人资金以及养老金领取者的资金”。美国财政部于 2023 年对卡特斯实施了制裁，原因是特朗普政府去年撤销了卡特斯的贿赂指控。
佩尼亚直到去年还持有一家与上野有关联的公司的股份，他表达了悔意。但他没有承认对这场动乱负责，这场动乱导致数百万储户、退休人员和工人争先恐后地收回被冻结的储蓄和拖欠的工资。
他说：“如果我在任何时候让人们失望了，我想向他们道歉。” “我从来没有打算背叛他们对我的信任。”
这场动荡已经打击了巴拉圭的货币。根据央行汇率数据，周四瓜拉尼兑美元汇率下跌近 4%，本周跌幅接近 7%。
上野银行在不到五年的时间里从一家名不见经传的金融公司发展成为家喻户晓的名字，拥有超过 60% 的巴拉圭成年人客户。许多巴拉圭人不禁要问，尽管一再对其放贷行为发出警告，但与总统有联系的银行为何规模和重要性能够如此迅速增长。
答案在于佩尼亚领导的科罗拉多党与该国监管机构和商界精英的关系令人不安，尽管稳定的经济管理和快速增长最近为巴拉圭赢得了令人垂涎的投资级信用评级，但这一弱点仍然存在。
“圣地亚哥·佩纳和科罗拉多党偷走了我们所有的积蓄，”周三游行到国会的抗议者之一路易斯·皮内达说。 “我们厌倦了70年的掠夺。”
2023 年获得银行牌照后不久，上野似乎就遍布巴拉圭的各个角落。这家数字贷款机构是一家拥有数十年历史的金融公司的更名版，通过慷慨的食品杂货现金返还优惠吸引客户，业务扩展到 70 多个地点，赞助巴拉圭国家足球队，并将自己的名字印在该国的主体育场上。
政府资金涌入佩纳领导下的上野的金库。他还任命上野银行前身 Financiera Ueno 行长卡洛斯·卡瓦洛 (Carlos Carvallo) 负责运营中央银行，该机构负责监管这家数字贷款机构。
截至上个月，上野报告称持有约 8 亿美元的公共存款，约占其总存款的四分之一，其中包括来自国家养老金和医疗基金以及巴拉圭巨型水力发电大坝运营商的资金。
尽管退休人员的储蓄和其他公共资金堆积在上野，央行内部的担忧仍在升级。据巴拉圭主要报纸 ABC Color 报道，今年 6 月，该公司的检查人员发现了向内部人士提供高风险贷款的模式。上野向与其所有者相关的公司提供了大量资金，超出了法律允许的范围，而且如果这些公司出现坏账，也没有足够的抵押品来偿还债务。
就在上个月，佩尼亚为上野和央行的监督进行了辩护，称这些担忧是一场吓唬公众的抹黑运动。

title_en: Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns
title_zh: 司法部民权办公室主任辞职
summary: The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, is out after 18 tumultuous months in charge.
summary_zh: 司法部民权司司长 Harmeet Dhillon 在经历了 18 个月的动荡任期后下台。
body_en: Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon, accompanied by her aides, speaks during a news conference at the Justice Department in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 29, 2025. Dhillon resigned on Thursday. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images hide caption

The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, is out after 18 tumultuous months in charge, during which she radically reshaped the unit's mission, oversaw the mass exodus of career staff, and aggressively pursued President Trump's agenda.
Dhillon is the first senior department official to depart the Trump administration since Democrats retook control of the House and Senate in midterm elections.
Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement on X, announced Dhillon's resignation and thanked her for her service.

"She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor," he wrote. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."
In her own statement, Dhillon said the job had been "the honor of a lifetime."
"We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women in girls' sports, and so much more," she added.
Reshaped civil rights mission at Justice Department transforms its work, workforce

During her tenure, Dhillon implemented dramatic changes in the Civil Rights Division, pushing out roughly 300 career attorneys, hiring inexperienced ideological allies to replace them, and using the division's enforcement powers to advance Trump's MAGA policies.

The changes marked a dramatic shift for the division, which was created some 70 years ago during the civil rights movement to end racial segregation in the U.S. For decades, it fought to protect the constitutional rights of all Americans across all aspects of life, from housing and employment to education and policing.

Dhillon, a conservative attorney and Trump loyalist, came into office with a different view. In her eyes, the division had narrowed its mission in recent decades to only protecting the rights of people of color, and she promptly shifted to aggressively pursuing conservative priorities.
"We don't just slow down the woke," she said at a Federalist Society event in 2025. "We take up the cause to achieve the executive branch's goals."
Trump's push to reshape the DOJ's civil rights division sparks mass exodus of attorneys

Under her leadership, the division redirected its energies to enforce Trump's executive orders, including ending the alleged radical indoctrination in schools, defending women from "gender ideology extremism," and combatting antisemitism and purported anti-Christian bias.
In the run-up to the midterm elections, the Civil Rights Division sued dozens of states demanding they turn over voter information — in furtherance of Trump's allegations of voter fraud.
Election officials pushed back, and courts tossed the department's lawsuits.

The division also accused numerous universities and law schools of discriminating against white and Asian students, and sued UCLA and Harvard for allegedly allowing antisemitism to flourish on campus.
Judge dismisses Trump administration's antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard
In an email to division staff, Dhillon said she informed Trump in early October that she planned to return to private practice after the midterms, and now is the time to do so.
body_zh: 2025 年 9 月 29 日，负责民权事务的助理司法部长哈米特·迪隆 (Harmeet Dhillon) 在助手的陪同下，在华盛顿特区司法部举行的新闻发布会上发表讲话。迪隆于周四辞职。安德鲁·哈尼克/盖蒂图片社隐藏标题栏
司法部民权司司长哈米特·迪伦 (Harmeet Dhillon) 在经历了 18 个月的混乱任期后离职，在此期间，她彻底重塑了该部门的使命，监督了职业员工的大规模外流，并积极推行特朗普总统的议程。
迪隆是自民主党在中期选举中重新控制众议院和参议院以来第一位离开特朗普政府的高级部门官员。
司法部长托德·布兰奇在 X 的一份声明中宣布迪隆辞职，并感谢她的服务。
他写道：“她捍卫了每个美国人的公民自由，并毫无恐惧或偏袒地执行法律。” “该部门感谢她热心的公共服务，我们祝愿她在未来的工作中一切顺利。”
迪隆在自己的声明中表示，这份工作是“一生的荣幸”。
“我们迎来了非法 DEI 的垮台，我们为保护女子体育运动中的女性而奋斗，等等，”她补充道。
司法部重塑民权使命改变其工作和员工队伍
在她的任期内，迪隆对民权部门实施了巨大的变革，解雇了大约 300 名职业律师，聘请了缺乏经验的意识形态盟友来取代他们，并利用该部门的执行权来推进特朗普的 MAGA 政策。
这些变化标志着该部门的巨大转变。该部门是在大约 70 年前结束美国种族隔离的民权运动期间创建的。几十年来，该部门一直致力于保护所有美国人在生活各个方面的宪法权利，从住房和就业到教育和治安。
迪隆是一名保守派律师，也是特朗普的忠实拥护者，他上任时持有不同的观点。在她看来，近几十年来，该部门已将其使命缩小到仅保护有色人种的权利，而她迅速转向积极追求保守派的优先事项。
她在 2025 年联邦党人协会的一次活动上表示：“我们不只是让人们慢下来。我们致力于实现行政部门的目标。”
特朗普推动重塑司法部民权部门引发律师大规模外流
在她的领导下，该部门将精力转向执行特朗普的行政命令，包括结束学校中所谓的激进灌输，保护妇女免受“性别意识形态极端主义”的侵害，以及打击反犹太主义和所谓的反基督教偏见。
在中期选举前夕，民权部门起诉数十个州，要求他们交出选民信息，以进一步证实特朗普关于选民欺诈的指控。
选举官员予以反击，法院也驳回了该部门的诉讼。
该部门还指控许多大学和法学院歧视白人和亚裔学生，并起诉加州大学洛杉矶分校和哈佛大学，指控其允许反犹太主义在校园内盛行。
法官驳回特朗普政府针对哈佛大学的反犹太主义诉讼
迪隆在给部门工作人员的一封电子邮件中表示，她于 10 月初通知特朗普，她计划在中期选举后重返私人诊所，现在是时候这样做了。

body_en: A federal judge temporarily blocked construction of President Trump's much-contested triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery, hours after the project received final planning approval.
Why it matters: The 14-day order halts the Trump administration's plans to begin work immediately on the 250-foot arch as the court considers lawsuits challenging the project's legality.

Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order early Friday barring construction of the arch for 14 days in response to a lawsuit brought by D.C. and Virginia.

The order prohibits construction, excavation, land disturbance, utility installation and road closures related to the arch. The administration must certify its compliance to the court by Monday, Nov. 9.

The backdrop: The ruling came hours after the National Capital Planning Commission — stacked with Trump loyalists — gave the project final approval Thursday during a packed virtual hearing that saw over 100 people testify and stretched over nine hours.
Opposing speakers included the D.C. Preservation League's executive director, military veterans and some of the family members of those buried at Arlington Cemetery.
Zoom in: The judge is considering separate legal challenges to the arch: One from D.C. and Virginia , and another from veterans.
The lawsuits argue that the administration lacks the necessary congressional authorization and has failed to comply with federal requirements.
The same judge earlier this week ordered that the government must notify the court within 30 minutes of beginning any activity related to arch construction.
The government has said that Maryland-based Grunley Construction Company might already be preparing to start construction in anticipation of sign-off.
The big picture: The proposed 250-foot arch has also been the source of fierce public objection and protests .
Critics have accused the administration of sidestepping necessary federal historic-preservation reviews and congressional sign-off, among other concerns.
Meanwhile, some Democratic lawmakers have suggested they'll make it harder for Trump to push his D.C. projects through once they assume Congressional control come January.

Between the lines: Critics of the project say it would overshadow and dishonor nearby Arlington Cemetery, snarl traffic during construction, hurt the local environment and create airspace safety issues at DCA, among other issues.
Building the project would take two to three years, with crews working 20 hours a day, per the administration.

What they're saying: The Trump administration has argued that the arch would improve the Arlington Cemetery visitor experience, as well as improve national security by containing drones and snipers, although final plans submitted to the NCPC didn't show these elements.
Trump earlier this week called the project "one of the great things we've ever done."
Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment early Friday.
Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan's ruling.

body_en: Russell Brand is convicted of rape. The judge says he'll get a prison term : NPR

Russell Brand is convicted of rape. The judge says he'll get a prison term A prosecutor described Brand as a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator." Brand, 51, denied the charges, saying he had never forced anyone to do something against their will.
Comedian and actor Russell Brand reflected in a car window as he left Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday. Alberto Pezzali/AP hide caption
London — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges involving four women on allegations dating back more than 20 years.

Judge Joel Bennathan said the British actor-comedian faces a "significant" prison term when he is sentenced Monday. Brand had been free, but the judge rejected a bail request because of the possibility he might flee and he was taken into custody.
"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."
Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator," prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said at trial.
Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.
He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand closed his eyes as the guilty verdict on the rape count was read but showed no emotion otherwise. When bail was denied, he gestured to his lawyers that he was OK and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken away.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London's Metropolitan Police said the conviction was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."
"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," he said. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."
The jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days.

Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004, but cleared of orally raping her in a restroom.
He was also found guilty of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 and of anally raping a fan he met backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009.
The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009.

Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party's annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men's bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.
body_zh: 拉塞尔·布兰德被判犯有强奸罪。法官称他将被判入狱：NPR
拉塞尔·布兰德被判犯有强奸罪。法官称他将被判入狱一名检察官将布兰德描述为一个冷酷无情、精于算计、善于操纵的“性掠夺者”。 51 岁的布兰德否认了这些指控，称他从未强迫任何人做违背自己意愿的事情。
周一，喜剧演员兼演员拉塞尔·布兰德离开伦敦南华克刑事法庭时，映在车窗里。阿尔贝托·佩扎利/美联社隐藏标题栏
伦敦——周四，拉塞尔·布兰德 (Russell Brand) 被判犯有强奸和性侵犯罪，涉及四名女性，这些指控可以追溯到 20 多年前。
乔尔·本纳森法官表示，这位英国喜剧演员周一被判刑时将面临“重大”监禁。布兰德已获释，但法官因他可能逃跑而拒绝了保释请求，因此被拘留。
“当然，我对给孩子们造成的困难感到遗憾，”法官说。 “但困难是由他们父亲的严重刑事犯罪造成的。”
检察官里尔·卡米-琼斯在审判中表示，布兰德是一个冷酷无情、精于算计、善于操纵的“性掠夺者”。
51 岁的布兰德否认了这些指控，并作证说，他年轻时沉迷于性，曾经过着放荡的生活，但从未强迫任何人做违背他们意愿的事情。
他被判犯有一项强奸罪和三项性侵犯罪。他的两项强奸罪名和一项企图猥亵罪名被判无罪。
当强奸罪的有罪判决被宣读时，布兰德闭上了眼睛，但没有表现出任何其他情绪。当保释被拒绝时，他向律师示意自己没事，并反复说：“我很好，我很好，我很好”，然后被带走。
伦敦大都会警察局侦探警司安迪·弗菲表示，这一定罪“证明了那些站出来报告自己遭遇的女性所具有的非凡勇气、韧性和决心。”
“布兰德利用他的影响力、地位和名气来剥削和性侵犯女性，”他说。 “随着他的知名度不断提高，他的权利意识也随之增强。”
南华克皇家法院的陪审团由八名男性和四名女性组成，在两天内审议了八个多小时。
布兰德以有伤风化的单口喜剧表演以及与毒品和酒精的斗争而闻名，他在 2000 年代初期声名鹊起，主持电视节目和自己的 BBC 广播节目。他出现在好莱坞电影中，包括《忘记莎拉·马歇尔》和《带他去希腊》，并与流行歌星凯蒂·佩里短暂结婚。
近年来，他离开了主流媒体，搬到了佛罗里达州，并通过混合健康、阴谋论和讨论他的宗教信仰的视频在网上建立了大批追随者。
布兰德因 2004 年在伦敦一家酒吧的生日派对上对一名女性进行性侵犯而被定罪，但在洗手间里对她进行口奸的罪名被免除。
他还被判犯有 2004 年或 2005 年在伦敦一家广播电台亲吻和猥亵另一名女子的罪名，以及 2009 年在一场喜剧节目后台强奸一名他在后台遇到的粉丝的罪名。
最终定罪的罪名是对另一名女性进行性侵犯，这名女性称这名喜剧演员在 2009 年录制广告时要求按摩，并将脸按在她的腹股沟上。
1999 年，布兰德在海边小镇伯恩茅斯举行的工党年度会议期间，在酒店房间内强奸了另一名妇女，并试图将一名妇女拖进音乐频道 MTV 伦敦办公室的男卫生间，对一名妇女进行猥亵，因此布兰德被判无罪。

title_en: Voters back abortion rights and reject Trump's redistricting in state ballot measures
title_zh: 随着各州就堕胎、重新划分选区和选民身份授权进行投票，特朗普的议程进入投票箱
summary: Abortion-rights advocates have achieved victories in Missouri, Nevada and Virginia
summary_zh: 选民正在决定有关堕胎权、国会选区重新划分和选民身份法的关键投票措施
